chapters.title: Chapter 938
paragraphs: “Has it been about fifty years?”
Jeok Cheongang murmured as he looked out over the garden, filled with rare flowers and plants of every color.
“Back then, Mount Li in Shaanxi looked just like this. It was the height of spring, and everything was in bloom.”
This wasn’t merely an old man reminiscing aloud. He was speaking to someone seated against a moss-covered wall.
“Mount Small Hua.”
“Hmm?”
“It was Mount Small Hua, not Mount Li.”
Her voice was calm and clear.
Jeok Cheongang shook his head at the Bow Saint’s correction.
“That can’t be right. I remember soaking in hot spring water. Mount Li’s been famous for its hot springs since ancient times.”
“It wasn’t a hot spring. It was a small pond—until someone said he couldn’t stand cold water and heated it with Scorching Yang Qi.”
“Did he?”
“You’ve completely forgotten how the Thunderbolt Saber King flew into a rage and nearly started a fight.”
“That Peng bastard?”
The Bow Saint nodded. Jeok Cheongang frowned.
“I don’t remember it, but he was an idiot then and he’s an idiot now. All that fuss over a little warm water.”
“He had good reason. The Thunderbolt Saber King was already in the pond.”
“He’s a big fellow. I must’ve mistaken him for a bear.”
The Bow Saint gave a small sigh at his shameless reply.
“You haven’t changed.”

“People aren’t so different from those flowers. Wind and rain batter them day and night, and a sudden change in their surroundings can kill them. If you want to live even one day longer, you have to stay the same—like this old man.”
“So you came to tell me the secret to a long life?”
“Does this old man look like he has that much time on his hands?”
“You showed up out of nowhere and started telling stories I’d rather not remember. You don’t look that busy.”
Jeok Cheongang smiled bitterly at her dry reply.
This time, he couldn’t disagree. No matter how he looked at it, those weren’t happy memories.
They’d gathered there one spring more than fifty years ago—not simply to laugh and talk. He couldn’t even remember the exact year now.
“Three thousand members of the death squad climbed that mountain together. Before a day had passed, half of them had been buried there.”
Mount Small Hua, green beneath the bright spring sky, had become a mountain of fire, dyed red from end to end.
He could still see it clearly: flames surging up the mountainside, blood mingling with the water in the valleys, and more corpses than he could count strewn everywhere.
The Zhongnan Sect. The Huashan Sect. The Hebei Peng Family.
And alongside them, smaller orthodox factions whose names had faded from people’s memories long ago.
The Blade of Flowers, Jin Baekyang—then the Second Young Master of the Jin Family of Taiyuan—had been there too.

The three thousand elite members of the death squad surged like a wave toward ten thousand Demonic Cult followers led by five great fiends. They broke against them, scattering blood instead of white foam.
At dawn, when the survivors stood atop a mountain of Demonic Cult corpses and shouted in victory, two kings and one star stood at their center.
“One thousand three hundred and nineteen.”
“That’s how many people died that day.”
Her quiet voice cut through the night air.
Jeok Cheongang stopped short, then slowly turned.
“You remember? All of them?”
Though his body had grown young again, the years remained in his eyes. And in those eyes, the woman’s gaze looked much like his own.
“I’ve never forgotten. Not for a moment.”
“...I didn’t know you were that kind of person.”
“Knowing changes nothing. All I do is remember them.”
The Bow Saint fell silent for a moment before adding, “That was simply the kind of time it was.”
Jeok Cheongang gave a faint nod.
“Yes. It was.”
The Demonic Cult’s momentum had been terrifying back then.
No—overwhelming.
The Hundred Thousand Demonic Disciples swept in like a wave, crushing the Kunlun Sect as they crossed Qinghai. Then they split into three forces and advanced unchecked.
Toward Sichuan. Toward Gansu. And beyond Shaanxi, into the heart of the continent known as the Central Plains.
Not even the Nine Sects and One Gang or the Five Great Families could stop that wave. The orthodox factions, still divided and guarding their own territories, crumbled almost at once.
The Demonic Cult’s long-cherished dream of a world ruled by the Demonic Path no longer seemed far-fetched.
Until one man appeared.
“Do you know what I was thinking the day I came down from Mount Jiuhua, after killing every last bastard who’d dared set it on fire?”
Jeok Cheongang didn’t wait for an answer.
“I swore to myself that until my dying breath, I’d kill as many Demonic Cult followers as I could.”
With the war already turning against them, taking on the Demonic Cult alone was madness.
The kind of madness only Jeok Cheongang, the Fire King, could attempt.
“But it turned out someone was even crazier than this old man.”
Jeok Cheongang laughed. He remembered preparing to charge straight at the Demonic Cult forces that had occupied Anhui after driving out even the Namgung Family.
“I just couldn’t believe it. Three thousand Demonic Cult followers defeated by one man.”

Those three thousand weren’t a rabble who’d barely risen above Third Rate. They were elites forged by the Demonic Cult’s brutal training, fanatics who had sworn absolute loyalty to the Heavenly Demon.
Among them were two great fiends who had reached the Supreme Peak realm.
“Of course, eventually I had no choice but to believe it.”

The story was too incredible to accept, so he’d caught several Demonic Cult followers as they fled and interrogated them. He confirmed that their two leading great fiends and nearly half their forces had vanished.
All because of someone no one could identify.
“That was when I remembered what my late Master used to say. The world is vast and there are many masters, so I must never stop striving.”
Before long, though, he understood.
Jeok Cheongang wasn’t lacking. That unknown man was exceptional.
No—beside him, anyone would have seemed ordinary.
“The Martial God.”
No one knew where he came from, what his name was, or how old he might be. Hardly anyone even knew his face.
He could wield every kind of martial art at will, and the disguise technique was no exception.
Yet everyone believed in him and followed him.
That was the kind of person he was. The only lamp lighting a world sunk in darkness. The sun, alone in the sky.
But precisely because of that, they could only circle him, instinctively unable to draw near.
They feared that the wind from a cautious outstretched hand might snuff out their only light.
Afraid that one step closer to the sun would leave them burning in its heat.
“So the Martial God’s identity remained a mystery to the very end. No—no one could even dare imagine it. Not even the Thousand-Faced Fox, who served him more closely than anyone.”
But now Jeok Cheongang knew the secret the world had never learned. At last, he understood why that man could be called the Martial God.
“Was it divine strength? That incomprehensible power.”
At his near-whisper, the Bow Saint slowly rose.
“Why? Are you planning to spread the word?”
“This old man’s only just started living like a proper person again. I won’t have people calling me senile.”
Jeok Cheongang gave a quiet laugh.
“So that’s why you kept talking when you knew I could hear you? Just because I’m that brat’s Master?”
“I simply saw no reason to hide it.”
The Bow Saint met his gaze.
“I saw you on the battlefield. A Master and Disciple willing to throw away their lives to save each other.”
“That was when I understood how much you trust each other. Hiding the truth would have been pointless.”

Jeok Cheongang answered calmly.

Jeok Cheongang cut her off. Her reflection appeared in his eyes, now dark and solemn.

Not because she hadn’t gotten the answer she wanted, but because she felt the air around them slowly heating up.

The wind stopped. The air trembled.

His Disciple might have grown strong enough to stand shoulder to shoulder with the Elders of great sects—perhaps even their Sect Leaders.
He might no longer be a rash young man like others his age, but someone with the stature to call himself a grandmaster.
Jin Taekyung was still his one and only Disciple.

White hellfire spiraled upward.

“Two thousand five hundred and sixty-two.”
Jeok Cheongang stopped in his tracks. He had been moving toward her, but he thought he knew what that unexpected number meant.
“That’s how many of our people died in the grand banquet hall three days ago.”
“You know the number well. But...”
His voice came out cold, utterly unlike the power blazing around him.
“If someone had stepped forward sooner, fewer than half of them would have died.”
“Yes. I’m sure you’re right.”
“What!”
*Whoosh.*
The flames around Jeok Cheongang burned hotter. The Bow Saint went on, unruffled.
“Even so, I had to see it with my own eyes. Whether that boy truly was the chosen one. What power he possessed, and what kind of person he was.”
“How dare you...!”
“After every battle, I counted the dead. It was one way I could remember them.”
“Shut your mouth!”
“But if ten times as many died as they did three days ago—one hundred times... No, more than a thousand times as many—could you still be angry as you are now?”
“To you, it may have been a trivial test that put your precious Disciple in danger. To me, it wasn’t.”
The Bow Saint looked into Jeok Cheongang’s trembling eyes.
“I made that decision for far more people than that. Perhaps for everyone in this world.”
“That was also why that person—the Martial God—chose me.”
Her soft murmur drifted through the cold night air.
*Step.*
Far away in the darkness came the faint sound of someone approaching.
They turned at the same time. Hyuk Mujin was running toward them with all his might.

“Did he?”

The Bow Saint nodded.

“He’s a big fellow.

The Bow Saint gave a small sigh at his shameless reply.

“So you came to tell me the secret to a long life?”

chapters.title: Chapter 939
paragraphs: *That guy...*
Jeok Cheongang recognized the familiar face hurrying toward them through the darkness and drew in the aura surging through his body.
Was it because the unexpected, unwelcome visitor was Hyuk Mujin?
No. Something about Mujin’s appearance was wrong.
*Huff, huff.*
His legs kept moving as he struggled for breath. Who knew how far he’d run? Sweat beaded on his face, and he looked desperate.
*...Something must have happened.*
Hoping his sudden sense of foreboding was mistaken, Jeok Cheongang called to Mujin, who had lost his bearings for a moment in the dark.
“What are you dawdling for?”
“Ah! Great Hero Jeok!”
Mujin rushed over, then stopped short when he spotted the Bow Saint.
“Th-this junior of Murim, Hyuk Mujin...”
The Bow Saint cut off his introduction with a small wave of her hand.
“Save the formalities. Tell us why you’re here.”
“It’s... Captain. I mean, my lord ordered me to bring the two of you to him at once.”
“The two of us?”
“Yes. I searched everywhere and couldn’t find either of you. When I asked my lord, he told me where to look...”
The Bow Saint’s brow furrowed.
But it wasn’t because a junior so far below her—Jin Taekyung, who was practically still a child—had dared to summon her as if he could order her around.
“He said he’d explain everything in person. Everyone else is already gathered.”
At that, the Bow Saint clicked her tongue softly.
“Something more serious than I thought must have happened. Serious enough for him to summon you and me.”
Jeok Cheongang nodded gravely.

Taekyung could be reckless, but within the bounds he observed, the brat was scrupulous about courtesy. If he had sent a subordinate to fetch even the Bow Saint, who was an outsider to him, Jeok Cheongang couldn’t begin to guess how serious the matter was.
—Unfortunately, I think we’ll have to end our conversation here.
The Bow Saint’s Sound Transmission reached his ear. Jeok Cheongang studied her calm face with a heavy gaze. She didn’t look the least bit disappointed.
—So it seems. For tonight.
He meant to continue the conversation another time. There were things he still hadn’t said and questions he hadn’t dared to ask. He had no intention of leaving it at this.
—I hope our next conversation will be more meaningful than this one.
Despite his pointed words, the Bow Saint remained composed.
—I’m sure it will be. Even if it isn’t next time, we’ll have plenty of chances.
—What do you mean by...
Jeok Cheongang faltered at the many possible meanings in her answer. He was just about to continue when—
*Flap, flap.*
The sound of powerful wings suddenly rang overhead.
*Those are...*
Jeok Cheongang looked up. The Bow Saint turned at the same moment, and Mujin followed their gazes.
*Whoosh!*
Dozens of birds crossed the distant night sky. They flew in separate groups, each bound in a different direction, moving with the precision of creatures thoroughly trained.
“Messenger eagles...!”
Jeok Cheongang spoke almost in a groan. A weight settled in his chest.
Sending out so many precious messenger eagles—not ordinary messenger pigeons—meant the Great Nation’s imperial court was on the move.
Probably because of the news his Disciple had brought.
*What could have happened?*
At least one thing was certain: there was no time left to hesitate.
“Lead the way. Hurry.”
The night was still far too deep for dawn. Yet unseen unrest was already sweeping through the Imperial Palace.
“What happened?”
Those were Jeok Cheongang’s first words as he swept in like the wind. Instead of answering, I held out what was in my hand.
*Swish.*
His gaze darkened at the sight of several sheets of paper, still slick with oil.
“A missive?”
A veteran martial artist whose experience was second to none in the world, he had immediately recognized the papers. He took the stack from me and skimmed through it quickly.
Before even a few moments had passed, he looked up, his face as hard as stone.
“Is everything written here... true?”
If it had been half an hour ago, I might not even have heard Jeok Cheongang’s voice.

But I’d since explained the situation to the Fire Dragon Pavilion members and passed the gist of it to Hong Jin and Qianqing Palace. I managed to answer calmly, though my answer was far from definite.
“I don’t know.”
“What do you mean!”
“To be precise, none of it has been confirmed yet. But...”
I looked from Jeok Cheongang’s rigid face to the Bow Saint, who was now reading the missive, and then to the Fire Dragon Pavilion members gathered inside the hall.
“The information is highly credible.”
“On what grounds?”
The Bow Saint set down the missive. Her gaze was graver than I’d ever seen it.
“No, before that—who sent it?”
“I don’t know that, either. Only that it was someone fairly high up in Dark Heaven.”
“How could someone like that send it to you...”
Her voice trailed off. Then she gave a low murmur.
“It wasn’t sent to you.”
Exactly. Whoever had written this missive had intended to pass the information to someone else.
“Could it be...?”
Jeok Cheongang spoke under his breath. I nodded.
“That’s right. It was among the things the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord kept.”
Their eyes widened. Even the Fire Dragon Pavilion members, who had heard the broad outline before Jeok Cheongang and the Bow Saint arrived, couldn’t hide their agitation.

Anyone who had read even one of those missives would react that way. The four or five sheets, still slick with oil, held information on which tens of thousands of lives depended. Maybe hundreds of thousands.
And one of them lay at my feet.
*Tap.*
I picked up the sheet with trembling fingers. Four characters caught my eye at once.
*Shanxi Annihilation Plan.*

At some unknown point in the past, someone had written to the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord: before the Double Ninth Festival, Dark Heaven’s main force would cross the vast northern grasslands and invade Shanxi Province.
*Crack.*
I clenched my teeth, swallowed a groan, and closed my eyes.
If—if this information was true...
*Just half a month.*
That was all the time left until the Double Ninth Festival.
All the time Shanxi Province had left. No—the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
Peace and turmoil went hand in hand.
Even in times of peace, disturbances great and small broke out somewhere in the world. And even amid the chaos of war, someone enjoyed peace.
That hadn’t changed when the long, fierce age of rival warlords ended and the Great Nation unified the land. It had always been true, was true now, and would remain true.
And nowhere in this vast world saw more constant strife than the northern grasslands.
A land of grass, earth, and horses. By day, birds rode the blue skies. By night, wild beasts huddled in the darkness and roamed in search of corpses.

Before the age of rival warlords, a nomadic people had conquered vast territories and called themselves rulers of the world. Their descendants still lived on those grasslands, in gers made of cloth and grass rather than splendid palaces or behind towering walls, alongside the horses that had been their constant companions since they first learned to walk.
Yet the glory their great ancestors had won was slowly fading from memory.
“Hmm. Not bad. No—excellent.”
The man spoke with satisfaction and took another drink.

Like other nomads, he had shaved the crown of his head and braided his remaining hair into a long queue. His imposing build and the golden crown on his forehead would have made him stand out above everyone else—if not for the man seated beside him in the place of honor.
“Temur, my brother. Have you forgotten that too much of anything can become poison?”
The other man had deep eyes and a lean build. He clicked his tongue softly at the hulking Temur. On his forehead sat another golden crown, this one engraved with two horses.
“You’re right, Chinggen. You always are.”
Temur nodded at Chinggen, who looked displeased, then grinned, baring yellow teeth.
“But remember one thing. Alcohol is medicine in itself. It can never be poison.”
“Oh, Temur.”
“Don’t be like that on a fine day. Have a drink with me, hmm?”
Chinggen shook his head. Temur jabbed him in the waist, raised his cup high, and called out, “What do you say, proud brothers of the grasslands?”
“Waaah!”
Hundreds of warriors cheered inside the vast ger. Temur roared with laughter.
“That’s more like it!”
He was happy. Two years ago, he had led fewer tribespeople than there were warriors in this ger. But look at him now.
He wore a golden crown. Instead of drinking mare’s-milk wine, made by milking horses and boiling the milk with his followers, he drank his fill of fine liquor brought from the distant Central Plains.
And all around him, the cheers poured in.
“Long live Khan Temur! Long live Khan Chinggen!”
“May you live to a ripe old age!”
Khan.
Ruler of the vast grasslands. King over tens of thousands of horses and warriors.
How good it sounded. The title that had once been only a dream was his now.
The two brothers, who had shared life and death, joy and sorrow since childhood, had brought peace and prosperity to the endlessly turbulent grasslands—and at last earned the title of Khan.
“Can you hear them? Hm? I said, are you listening?”
Temur, who had been mingling with his warriors, filled Chinggen’s empty cup.

It was silver, imported from the Central Plains rather than carved from wood or animal bone. Its gleaming surface reflected both their faces: Temur’s broad grin and Chinggen’s unmistakable discomfort.
“Of course I hear them. But this isn’t the time to laugh and drink, Temur.”
“Good grief, there you go again. Since when does laughing and drinking need a special occasion?”
“My brother, didn’t I send a messenger with news?”
“Ah, that? I heard.”
Temur chewed noisily on a piece of meat as he continued.
“But don’t worry so much. We may be Khans now, but the grasslands are vast. We can’t do anything about what happens beyond our reach.”
Of course Temur knew. A few scouts had gone missing from time to time, and there had been several disturbances on the westernmost grasslands.
Not enough to make him forget the indulgence of the moment.
“Come, my ever-worried brother. Let’s empty our cups first, then talk.”
Temur laughed heartily and was about to offer Chinggen another drink when—
*Flap.*
A cold wind laden with sandy dust pushed open the entrance to the ger.

The sound of powerful wings suddenly rang overhead.
*Those are...*
Jeok Cheongang looked up.
The Bow Saint turned at the same moment, and Mujin followed their gazes.
*Whoosh!*
Dozens of birds crossed the distant night sky.
They flew in separate groups, each bound in a different direction, moving with the precision of creatures thoroughly trained.
“Messenger eagles...!”
Jeok Cheongang spoke almost in a groan.
A weight settled in his chest.
Sending out so many precious messenger eagles—not ordinary messenger pigeons—meant the Great Nation’s imperial court was on the move.
Probably because of the news his Disciple had brought.
*What could have happened?*
At least one thing was certain: there was no time left to hesitate.
“Lead the way.
Hurry.”
The night was still far too deep for dawn.
Yet unseen unrest was already sweeping through the Imperial Palace.
“What happened?”
Those were Jeok Cheongang’s first words as he swept in like the wind.
Instead of answering, I held out what was in my hand.
*Swish.*
His gaze darkened at the sight of several sheets of paper, still slick with oil.
“A missive?”
A veteran martial artist whose experience was second to none in the world, he had immediately recognized the papers.
He took the stack from me and skimmed through it quickly.
Before even a few moments had passed, he looked up, his face as hard as stone.
“Is everything written here... true?”
If it had been half an hour ago, I might not even have heard Jeok Cheongang’s voice.
But I’d since explained the situation to the Fire Dragon Pavilion members and passed the gist of it to Hong Jin and Qianqing Palace.
I managed to answer calmly, though my answer was far from definite.
“I don’t know.”
“What do you mean!”
“To be precise, none of it has been confirmed yet.
But...”
I looked from Jeok Cheongang’s rigid face to the Bow Saint, who was now reading the missive, and then to the Fire Dragon Pavilion members gathered inside the hall.
“The information is highly credible.”
“On what grounds?”
The Bow Saint set down the missive.
Her gaze was graver than I’d ever seen it.
“No, before that—who sent it?”
“I don’t know that, either.
Only that it was someone fairly high up in Dark Heaven.”
“How could someone like that send it to you...”
Her voice trailed off.
Then she gave a low murmur.
“It wasn’t sent to you.”
Exactly.
Whoever had written this missive had intended to pass the information to someone else.
“Could it be...?”
Jeok Cheongang spoke under his breath.
I nodded.
“That’s right.
It was among the things the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord kept.”
Their eyes widened.
Even the Fire Dragon Pavilion members, who had heard the broad outline before Jeok Cheongang and the Bow Saint arrived, couldn’t hide their agitation.
Anyone who had read even one of those missives would react that way.
The four or five sheets, still slick with oil, held information on which tens of thousands of lives depended.
Maybe hundreds of thousands.
And one of them lay at my feet.
*Tap.*
I picked up the sheet with trembling fingers.
Four characters caught my eye at once.
*Shanxi Annihilation Plan.*

At some unknown point in the past, someone had written to the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord: before the Double Ninth Festival, Dark Heaven’s main force would cross the vast northern grasslands and invade Shanxi Province.
*Crack.*
I clenched my teeth, swallowed a groan, and closed my eyes.
If—if this information was true...
*Just half a month.*
That was all the time left until the Double Ninth Festival.
All the time Shanxi Province had left.
No—the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
Peace and turmoil went hand in hand.
Even in times of peace, disturbances great and small broke out somewhere in the world.
And even amid the chaos of war, someone enjoyed peace.
That hadn’t changed when the long, fierce age of rival warlords ended and the Great Nation unified the land.
It had always been true, was true now, and would remain true.
And nowhere in this vast world saw more constant strife than the northern grasslands.
A land of grass, earth, and horses.
By day, birds rode the blue skies.
By night, wild beasts huddled in the darkness and roamed in search of corpses.
Before the age of rival warlords, a nomadic people had conquered vast territories and called themselves rulers of the world.

Their descendants still lived on those grasslands, in gers made of cloth and grass rather than splendid palaces or behind towering walls, alongside the horses that had been their constant companions since they first learned to walk.
Yet the glory their great ancestors had won was slowly fading from memory.
“Hmm.
Not bad.
No—excellent.”
The man spoke with satisfaction and took another drink.
Like other nomads, he had shaved the crown of his head and braided his remaining hair into a long queue.
His imposing build and the golden crown on his forehead would have made him stand out above everyone else—if not for the man seated beside him in the place of honor.
“Temur, my brother.
Have you forgotten that too much of anything can become poison?”
The other man had deep eyes and a lean build.
He clicked his tongue softly at the hulking Temur.
On his forehead sat another golden crown, this one engraved with two horses.
“You’re right, Chinggen.
You always are.”
Temur nodded at Chinggen, who looked displeased, then grinned, baring yellow teeth.
“But remember one thing.
Alcohol is medicine in itself.
It can never be poison.”
“Oh, Temur.”
“Don’t be like that on a fine day.
Have a drink with me, hmm?”
Chinggen shook his head.
Temur jabbed him in the waist, raised his cup high, and called out, “What do you say, proud brothers of the grasslands?”
“Waaah!”
Hundreds of warriors cheered inside the vast ger.
Temur roared with laughter.
“That’s more like it!”
He was happy.
Two years ago, he had led fewer tribespeople than there were warriors in this ger.
But look at him now.
He wore a golden crown.
Instead of drinking mare’s-milk wine, made by milking horses and boiling the milk with his followers, he drank his fill of fine liquor brought from the distant Central Plains.
And all around him, the cheers poured in.
“Long live Khan Temur!
Long live Khan Chinggen!”
“May you live to a ripe old age!”
Khan.
Ruler of the vast grasslands.
King over tens of thousands of horses and warriors.
How good it sounded.
The title that had once been only a dream was his now.
The two brothers, who had shared life and death, joy and sorrow since childhood, had brought peace and prosperity to the endlessly turbulent grasslands—and at last earned the title of Khan.
“Can you hear them?
Hm?
I said, are you listening?”
Temur, who had been mingling with his warriors, filled Chinggen’s empty cup.
It was silver, imported from the Central Plains rather than carved from wood or animal bone.
Its gleaming surface reflected both their faces: Temur’s broad grin and Chinggen’s unmistakable discomfort.
“Of course I hear them.
But this isn’t the time to laugh and drink, Temur.”
“Good grief, there you go again.
Since when does laughing and drinking need a special occasion?”
“My brother, didn’t I send a messenger with news?”
“Ah, that?
I heard.”
Temur chewed noisily on a piece of meat as he continued.
“But don’t worry so much.
We may be Khans now, but the grasslands are vast.
We can’t do anything about what happens beyond our reach.”
Of course Temur knew.
A few scouts had gone missing from time to time, and there had been several disturbances on the westernmost grasslands.
Not enough to make him forget the indulgence of the moment.
“Come, my ever-worried brother.
Let’s empty our cups first, then talk.”
Temur laughed heartily and was about to offer Chinggen another drink when—
*Flap.*
A cold wind laden with sandy dust pushed open the entrance to the ger.

paragraphs: While a ger on the grasslands shivered in the cool night wind, heavy with sand, people behind a massive wall ten thousand li away were greeting the morning.
The sun was still a long way from rising. Darkness surrounded them on every side.
*Thudthudthudthud!*
Rough hoofbeats shattered the silence of the night.

More than a hundred messengers passed through the Seven Gates without a single formality. Like the dozens of messenger eagles sent ahead of them, they vanished into the wind, each bound for a different destination.
The man who had given all these orders listened, pale-faced, as reports came in one after another.
“All the messengers have just passed through the Seven Gates!”
“The Imperial Decree has been delivered to the high ministers of the Six Ministries!”
“The Censorate awaits Your Majesty’s command!”
“The officials of the Hanlin Academy and the Transmission Office are preparing the edict!”
“A report from the Five Tiger Commandery! In accordance with Your Majesty’s command, we are immediately mobilizing three hundred warships, one hundred thousand naval troops, and the Imperial Guards—”
“Enough.”
At the Emperor’s sudden command, every sound around him vanished as if washed away.
The Son of Heaven’s authority was absolute.
Though the Great Nation was only in its third generation, the power wielded by its current Emperor equaled—or perhaps surpassed—that of Taizu, who had unified the realm.
“How noisy.”
At the Emperor’s quiet murmur, everyone prostrated themselves, barely daring to breathe.
“We beg Your Majesty’s forgiveness!”
“Please execute us!”
*Rustle.*
The Emperor gave a small shake of his head and silently waved his long sleeve.
Those who understood the unspoken command backed away and disappeared with careful steps. Before long, only two people remained in the vast main hall.
“Every time I say anything, they start begging me to kill them. If I’d had to listen to that for another fifteen minutes, I might’ve bitten through my own tongue.”
At the Emperor’s bitter smile, Baek Yeon, Commander of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, spoke with a stern expression.
“Even as a joke, please don’t say such things.”
“It’s only a joke. What does it matter? Besides...”
The Emperor leaned at an angle against the throne and continued.
“I have not the slightest intention of dying in a situation like this.”
His face was still pale, but as he faced a new crisis, his eyes gleamed like luminous pearls.
“I expected as much, but it’s worse than I thought. I didn’t think they’d move so quickly.”
Baek Yeon wholeheartedly agreed.
Dark Heaven.
That rebellious faction, whose very name was ominous, was larger than expected—and more methodical, too.
Even more so than a religious movement that had once erupted like a grass fire from a distant western land, back when Baek Yeon had served the late Emperor.
“It was more than fifty years ago that those called the Demonic Cult headed for the Central Plains.”
“The Great Faction War.”
The Emperor murmured to himself and stroked his graying beard.
Though it had happened long before he was born, everyone knew of the momentous event when no fewer than a hundred thousand cultists set foot in the Central Plains.
Especially because they weren’t merely country bumpkins lured in by sweet words. They were an army armed with unwavering faith and spears and swords.

“When the Demonic Cult’s momentum reached the heavens, the martial artists of the orthodox factions petitioned the late Emperor. They said the Demonic Cult was a foreign enemy disrupting the Great Nation’s order, and asked him to raise the Imperial Army and order a campaign against them.”
“I know.”
The Emperor looked at Baek Yeon and added,
“And I know you opposed joining the war more strongly than anyone.”
Baek Yeon gave a small nod in acknowledgment.
It was true.

Here, in this very place, the high ministers of the court had argued fiercely for days. The late Emperor had seriously considered ordering a campaign, but Baek Yeon had pleaded with him more earnestly than ever before, and the Emperor had finally given up the idea.
“Can Your Majesty guess why I opposed it so strongly?”
“I think there were two main reasons. First, the Demonic Cult feared the Great Nation’s power and wasn’t harming the people. And second... Cang Gong.”
“That’s right. Unlike me, Cang Gong was the first to insist that we drive out the foreign enemy.”
“You made the right choice. If Father had sided with Cang Gong back then, the Great Nation would have shed a great deal of blood.”
“It was clear he intended to weaken the imperial house. That was all the more reason I had to oppose it.”
There had never been a victory without wounds, not in all of history.
Baek Yeon knew that as a commander who led an army, not merely as a martial artist. He had done everything in his power to keep the Great Nation out of the war.
Cang Gong—or rather, the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord—had already been someone to watch back then.
Of course, countless orthodox martial artists had died because of Baek Yeon’s opposition. But he didn’t regret it in the least.
He had simply made the choice that was best for the Emperor and the Great Nation—and, by extension, the people.
It wouldn’t have been too late to intervene after watching the two great powers, the Murim Alliance and the Demonic Cult, crash violently into each other.
And the result of that wait had been an orthodox victory that came close to mutual destruction.
“Back then, I actually hoped the Demonic Cult would win.”
The Emperor clicked his tongue at Baek Yeon’s words.
“You’re unusually honest today.”

“It can’t be helped. Many martial artists of the orthodox factions have the people’s trust, so we’d have no grounds to launch a campaign against them. But it would’ve been different if the Demonic Cult had survived.”
A massive boulder was too heavy even to move.
But what about a pebble left behind after being smashed and battered again and again?
And if that pebble had jagged edges sharp enough to harm the people, Baek Yeon would have taken up his hammer without the slightest hesitation.
He would have torn down the lawless fence that was Murim once and for all.
“But if things had gone as you hoped, we wouldn’t have made it to the present day.”
The Emperor’s low voice echoed through the vast hall.
He was right. It was deeply ironic, but they had relied on those very martial artists to put down the traitors and accomplish their great undertaking.
And now... it was time to set that contradiction right.
“I intend to help with everything I have. For their sake—and for all of us.”
*Thump.*
Baek Yeon lowered his head and went down on one knee.
A storm of bloodshed would soon descend, one that would dwarf the Great Faction War.
Dark Heaven was more powerful than the Demonic Cult, and incomparably more dangerous.
A war was beginning that would not be confined to Murim. It would overturn the world.
“Your Majesty, ruler of all beneath the heavens, I humbly ask that you give me your orders.”
The information Jin Taekyung had delivered in the dead of night was an unexpected misfortune. Fortunately, they had already made thorough preparations to accomplish their great undertaking.
Hundreds of warships and thousands of officers.
Hundreds of thousands of troops, the imperial banners flying above them, were waiting for their command.
“I command Baek Yeon, Commander of the Embroidered Uniform Guard.”
Speaking in a solemn voice, the Emperor slowly rose despite his ailing body.
Instead of his white sleeping robe embroidered with a golden dragon, he wore heavy armor. He strode across the hall without hesitation.
*Clank. Clank.*
One step. Then another.
The Emperor descended from the throne and personally raised Baek Yeon to his feet.
“Tell the entire army that I will lead the campaign in person.”
Baek Yeon’s eyes trembled for an instant, unable to hide his shock.
It wasn’t only the impact of the Emperor taking command in person. He could feel the resolve of a man who had little time left to live.
“Your Majesty.”
But the words Baek Yeon struggled to force out never came.
Seeing the Emperor silently shake his head, the loyal subject could only clench his teeth, his heart heavy.
“I, Baek Yeon, Commander of the Embroidered Uniform Guard... will obey Your Majesty’s solemn command.”
The Emperor gave him a faint smile instead of an answer, then walked past him.
The world beyond the wide-open iron gates was still shrouded in darkness.
Like his own future, with so little of it left.
*Still, this isn’t so bad.*
His body might be dying, but his mind was clearer than ever.
The first campaign he would lead in person—and the last.
To meet his end on a battlefield instead of in bed would be a blessing, not a tragedy.
And so was the fact that someone had brought back his will to live, if only for a while.
“Come, Baek Yeon.”
The Emperor smiled brightly—so brightly it was hard to believe he was a dying man—and continued,
“We should see off a certain insolent rogue who’s leaving before me without keeping his promise to me.”
One shichen.
That was how much time had passed since I’d first gotten my hands on the iron chest left behind by the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord.
“Everything’s ready.”
At Hyuk Mujin’s report in my ear, I opened my eyes, which I’d kept tightly shut.
His gaze and expression were unusually grave. That alone said how urgent things had become.
“Let’s go.”
What else was there to say?
I gave a brief reply and stepped out of the pavilion, moving as if in a daze.
Even after circulating my qi once, my mind was still a mess.
*Half a month.*
Only half a month.
That was all the time left until the Double Ninth Festival. Or maybe even less.
The missive the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord had kept said Dark Heaven’s main force would invade Shanxi Province through the northern grasslands before the festival.
*It could be ten days. No—even tomorrow.*
I swallowed the groan rising in my throat.
This wasn’t just urgent. It was an emergency.
The distance from here, Zhejiang Province, where the Imperial Capital stood, to Shanxi Province was a full ten thousand li.
No matter how quickly the Imperial Court’s messenger eagles flew, the trip would take at least ten days.
*Can I get there in time?*
Even as I left the imperial palace with everyone else, doubt weighed heavily on my heart.
Then Jeok Cheongang, who had been watching me in silence the whole time, suddenly spoke.
“Was it about fifty years ago? I got into some petty dispute with that Thunderbolt Saber King bastard and ended up in a real fight.”
As though he were talking to himself, Jeok Cheongang glanced away from me and continued.
“I’d always looked down on him as someone far beneath me, so I didn’t think much of him. But when we actually traded blows, he was pretty strong. I didn’t show it, but I was surprised.”
The Bow Saint, who had been riding quietly with the reins in hand, replied.
“He’s a strong man. If it hadn’t been for you, he probably would’ve been the greatest of the Ten Kings.”
“Hmm. I suppose so.”
Jeok Cheongang nodded, then glanced at me and added,

“Still, the Hebei Peng Family didn’t become one of the Five Great Families for no reason. With that kind of strength, they could beat just about anyone. And they have enough intelligence-gathering power to keep a clear eye on what’s happening not only in Hebei but in Shanxi, too.”
Only then did I think I understood.
This completely random conversation was meant to put me at ease.
*Heh.*
What was I supposed to say? I was just grateful.
And just as I swallowed the laugh threatening to slip out, someone spoke.
“So, were you planning to leave just like this without saying goodbye?”
The breezy voice didn’t suit him at all. The Emperor, who had been waiting for me in front of the enormous iron gates, laughed aloud.

The breezy voice didn’t suit him at all.
The Emperor, who had been waiting for me in front of the enormous iron gates, laughed aloud.

chapters.title: Chapter 941
paragraphs: An endless stretch of city wall. A massive iron gate controlling passage to the north.
And at the head of a thousand Embroidered Uniform Guards and several court ministers standing in formation on either side, imperial banners embroidered with dragons held high, stood one man.
“So, were you planning to leave just like this without saying goodbye?”
The Emperor’s sudden appearance caught me off guard. Then I returned his smile with a faint one of my own.
“Your Majesty.”
“I hope I’m not taking up your precious time.”
“My time is precious, but I can spare a little of it for a meeting worth having. As it happens, there’s something I need to tell you in person, too.”
The Emperor tilted his head, not quite grasping what I meant, then smacked his lips.
“You sound as if you knew I’d be waiting.”
“Honestly, I didn’t expect that. But I’m glad to see you, even like this.”
“Enough of that empty flattery. It doesn’t suit you.”
The Emperor feigned a frown, then jerked his chin over his shoulder.
“Why not answer honestly, like you usually do? It isn’t me you’re glad to see. It’s them.”
He was right.
The Emperor wasn’t the only one waiting for me in front of the Imperial Capital’s North Gate.
*That’s...*
Familiar faces came into view.
The Thousand Captain of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, Jeong Hogun—the first face I’d seen at the imperial court, and the one I’d seen most often since—was only the beginning.
Baek Yeon and Hong Jin, who should have been busier than anyone else right now, were there too. And I spotted someone I hadn’t seen in days.
*Prince Shangshan. No—the Imperial Younger Brother.*
Warmth spread through a corner of my heart. That boy, whose life had once hung by a thread, was now with his only family.
And I’d get to say goodbye before I left.
I gave Zhu Bao, who sat in his saddle looking ready to burst into tears, a faint smile. Then I turned back to the Emperor.
“May I answer honestly, as you said?”
“No, never mind. I’ve changed my mind.”
“I’ve changed mine too. You’re right—I’m happier to see them than I am to see Your Majesty.”
“How dare you...!”
His suppressed voice was accompanied by an air that instantly turned cold.
But after glaring at me for a moment, the Emperor burst into the laughter he’d been holding back.
“You never cease to amaze me. No—it’s downright bizarre. How can you be so arrogant and rude to the father of all the people and the supreme ruler?”
“As I’ve already told you, I’m just a rogue. I don’t even have an identity plaque, and I have parents of my own.”
Gasps sounded here and there.
Most of the people—especially the court ministers who had no idea why they were even here—looked at one another as if to ask whether this was really happening.
The Emperor, of course, was still smiling.
“I see. You are neither my subject nor a citizen of the Great Nation.”
Without waiting for my reply, he continued.
“But you think and act according to justice, righteousness, and chivalry. You are truly a hero of your age, worthy of the admiration of all.”
*Clip-clop. Clip-clop.*
The Emperor rode slowly toward me until he was right in front of me. He gazed at me for a moment, then suddenly raised a hand to his shoulder.
*Slip. Thump.*
The tightly tied cord came loose. Without hesitation, the Emperor removed his cloak and held it out to me with a faint smile.
“What are you waiting for? Take it.”
An unseen shockwave swept through everyone.
The court ministers trembled as if they’d suffered strokes, staring aghast at the cloak embroidered with a golden dragon that looked ready to come alive.
“Y-Your Majesty!”
“T-That is...!”
Shouts came from every direction.
But their desperate voices were swallowed by the wind at the Emperor’s curt command.
“Enough.”
In the heavy silence pressing down on those around us, the Emperor turned his gaze to me and spoke.
“Go on. It’s just a little gift from me.”
I looked from the Emperor, who was urging me on, to the cloak in his hand. All I could do was blink.
Even without everyone’s reaction, I knew this was no ordinary gift.
“This is... a lot more than a little gift.”
It was no ordinary cloak.
The Emperor himself had worn it. That alone would have made it extraordinary. But something else mattered even more.
A dragon.
A single dragon embroidered on the cloak in golden thread.
Even a three-year-old knew it was the emblem of the Son of Heaven and the imperial house’s authority.
“You seem to know what it means.”
I answered in disbelief.
“How could I not?”
“Good. Then you’ll be all the more eager to accept this precious gift before my hand falls off.”
“Wait, wait a moment.”
The sudden turn of events had me hesitating, but the Emperor was firm.
“Please don’t refuse. If you do, something will happen that you’ll deeply regret.”
“What?”
I stared at him blankly. The Emperor continued in a deliberately stern voice.
“If you refuse even this, I’ll be very hurt.”
“What does that—”
“No one can say what might happen. But rest assured. Surely I wouldn’t make the imperial house’s Benefactor uncomfortable over something so trivial?”
“Is it just me, or was none of that reassuring?”
“Exactly. It’s just you.”
The Emperor and I stared at each other in silence for a while.
Then, as if we’d agreed to it, we both let out a dry chuckle.
We hadn’t known each other long, but we already understood.
Maybe, just a little...
*We were alike.*
I had fought to protect what was precious to me. He, too, had made sacrifices for someone else.
He’d wagered his life without hesitation, and he didn’t regret it.
The only difference was where we stood and what we saw. Just like me, the Emperor was only human.
Someone who knew how to be grateful for help, who liked jokes, who feared death.
One person who had fought as best he could from the place where he stood.
*Swish.*
I reached out, took the cloak the Emperor offered, and draped it over my shoulders. Then I respectfully clasped my hands in a salute.
“I gratefully accept this precious gift.”
“It suits you. But there’s one thing missing.”
The Emperor looked at me in the cloak with satisfaction, then took a gleaming silver plaque from between the plates of his armor and held it out.
The next words made me doubt my ears.
“By the authority of the Son of Heaven, I name Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan Marquis of Shangshan!”
His voice, strengthened with internal energy, broke the deep-night silence.
As his declaration rang out, commoners who had watched the imperial procession from afar, not daring to approach, began gathering around the torches held by the Embroidered Uniform Guards.
The Emperor continued in a solemn voice.

“I grant you as your fief more than ten counties in Shanxi Province, including Taiyuan, Honju, Yangcheon, Jeongyang, Jinzhong, Taigu, and Jiaocheng, along with the revenues of ten thousand households and a hundred thousand taels of gold and silver. In addition...”
*Shing.*
A flash of light suddenly leapt from his waist. The Emperor drew the imperial sword, his eyes gleaming as he shouted,

“From this moment, I also grant you the post of Thousand Captain of the Embroidered Uniform Guard. Lead a thousand guards and, by imperial command, swiftly put down the foreign bandits who disturb the order of the realm!”
I could hardly breathe. My chest thudded.
*Thump. Thump. Thump!*
That wasn’t my heartbeat.
The thousand Embroidered Uniform Guards standing in formation on either side stamped their feet with all their might. They clashed their weapons together and struck their armor.
For the Emperor.
No—for me.
*Ah.*
I swallowed the groan rising in my throat.
Only now did I understand.
The Emperor hadn’t brought a thousand Embroidered Uniform Guards here to wait for me merely as an escort.
They were a force assembled by imperial command to punish the enemy.
And they were reinforcements he’d prepared for me.
A shield and a sword to defend Shanxi Province and the Jin Family of Taiyuan against Dark Heaven.
“Waaaah!”
*Ding. Ding-ding.*
My ears rang with the ceaseless chiming of bells and the shouts and cheers erupting all around me.
And there, at the center of it all, the Emperor smiled at me.
“Success makes you a king; failure makes you a traitor.”
Two had plotted a revolution, but only one had survived.
The Emperor had uprooted the traitors and put everything back in its place. Now he was rewarding those about to depart.
“Every deed has its due. What do you think of the gift I prepared?”
What more could I say?
I let out the breath I’d been holding.
“It’s incredible.”
“As a marquis, you should rightfully be my subject, but I don’t care about that.”
*Tap.*
The Emperor’s hand came to rest on my shoulder. The spark of life within him was slowly going out, yet I could feel the warmth of his fingertips.
“Go on as you have until now.”
“Keep your eyes on what is right. Let your intentions and actions follow righteousness and chivalry.”
His voice flowed on, and he added quietly,
“Be neither my subject nor my citizen... Just be someone who shines a light upon this world.”
His words, low and heavy, rang in my ears like a final testament.
Meeting and parting are inseparable.
Where there’s a meeting, there’s a parting; and after a parting, another meeting awaits.
Even so, the moment of parting is always bitter and full of regret.
Especially for a child saying goodbye to someone he had relied on so deeply.
*Tap. Drip.*
Moisture fell onto the saddle.
Rather than look at his youngest brother’s silently weeping face, the Emperor gazed at the empty places left by those who had departed and spoke calmly.
“Are you that sad?”
“N-no, I’m not.”
Zhu Bao hurriedly wiped his eyes with his sleeve.
A child was allowed to cry, but the Imperial Younger Brother was different.
As heir to the Great Nation, Zhu Bao would have to face the coming war. He had become someone who must never cry.
“I’m not sad at all.”
“That’s very strange.”
“Pardon?”
“I’m sorry to see them go. How can you, not even fifteen yet, feel no sadness?”
Zhu Bao looked up in surprise. The Emperor’s smiling face was reflected clearly in his eyes.
“Bao’er.”
Zhu Bao stared at him, too stunned to answer. The Emperor spoke gently.
“You needn’t start swallowing your feelings already.”
“They say endurance is bitter and its fruit sweet. But endurance that piles up like that will turn to poison one day.”
“H-hyung. I mean, Your Majesty.”
“When you want to cry, cry as much as you like.”
*Tap.*
With an awkward hand, the Emperor stroked Zhu Bao’s head. Then he turned his horse around and rode away.
He repeated something someone had once told him.
“You and I are both human, in the end.”
As sobs rose behind him, the Emperor hoped that Zhu Bao—his youngest brother, at least—would not follow in his footsteps.
*I... realized far too late.*
A faint smile touched the Emperor’s lips. Just then, a fine horse came galloping through the enormous iron gate as it slowly closed.
*Wait. That man...*
Amid a situation he couldn’t understand, the Emperor saw the man who had returned and asked,
“Did you leave something behind, Divine Physician?”
“Yes.”
The Divine Physician smiled and continued,
“I left a patient behind.”

chapters.title: Chapter 942
paragraphs: “I left a patient behind.”
At the Divine Physician’s answer, the Emperor’s eyes trembled.
*Could it be...?*
Suddenly, he found it hard to breathe. Without realizing it, he clenched both fists.
A spark of hope kindled in a heart he’d thought he’d emptied completely. He could feel his resolve wavering—the resolve to die on a battlefield, not in his bedchamber.
*No. It can’t be.*
But deep down, the Emperor could only shake his head. A crisis could drive a person to the edge of a cliff. Hope was what finally sent them plunging into the abyss.
And so he forced himself to look away from the Divine Physician, who still watched him with a gentle smile.
“If you intend to join the army, I won’t stop you. Before long, there will be countless casualties. Your medical skills will be put to good use.”
“Your Majesty.”
Leaving the Divine Physician to finish whatever he’d meant to say, the Emperor quietly turned away.
Jin Taekyung, who had left to protect the Jin Family of Taiyuan, wasn’t the only one with no time to spare.
The Emperor’s life was truly drawing to a close. In the brief time he had left—a few months at most—he meant to do everything he could.
For a better future.
For the precious people who would remain in this world after he was gone.
*That is my sole duty.*
The moment he steeled his resolve again, a quiet voice sounded behind him.
“I understand, Your Majesty. I know how you feel.”
*Thud.*
The Emperor stopped as if his feet had been nailed to the ground.
The Divine Physician’s voice continued in his ear.
“A fleeting hope must frighten you. Nothing is more painful than false hope.”
After a brief silence, the Emperor slowly turned. The Divine Physician was still smiling at him.
“You understand well.”
“Through no choice of my own.”
“You must have met countless people standing between life and death in your work as a physician.”
“That’s not the only reason.”
“Then what is?”
The Divine Physician’s smile faded.
“A very long time ago, there was a young carpenter.”
“A carpenter? Did he come to you because he had a fatal illness, too?”
“More precisely, he came to save his wife and children from an epidemic.”
“...His wife and children.”

“He carried his feverish wife and two children on his back in a wooden carrying frame. For three days and nights, he climbed the mountain without sleep, looking for a skilled physician said to be staying in a nearby slash-and-burn farming village.”
The Emperor pictured the carpenter, drenched in sweat as he climbed the mountain, and muttered,
“That must have been hard. Very hard.”
“As you say, it surely was.”
“But I doubt he even felt how exhausted he was. He had hope he could save his family.”
The Divine Physician nodded.
“Yes. He didn’t set down the frame and collapse until he reached his destination. Then he lay sick for a day and a half.”
“So, did you treat his family?”
“Unfortunately, I couldn’t.”
The Emperor gave a small sigh. The Divine Physician added bitterly,
“By the time I regained consciousness, it was too late.”
“That’s why I know how cruel hope can be. What kind of despair waits at the bottom of that cliff.”
The Emperor fell silent.
He looked at the old physician before him, seeing the young carpenter who had lost his wife and children to an epidemic long ago and chosen a new path. After a long while, he spoke.
“Then... then have you truly...?”
His voice shook with emotion he could not hide. He forced out the question he’d wanted to ask from the start.
“Have you found a way to treat Us?”
Light returned to his eyes, and hope crept into his voice.
The Divine Physician bowed deeply.
“Yes. With the help of Heaven—or rather, Young Master Jin—I was able to find the one and only path to survival.”
Jin Taekyung.
The unexpected name made the Emperor close his eyes. In the darkness, he pictured Jin Taekyung’s face and offered him thanks he would never hear.
*You didn’t forget your promise to Us.*
He had not resented Jin Taekyung for leaving. Even when he’d watched him walk away without a word about their promise, he’d felt only gratitude for all Jin Taekyung had done for the imperial house.
He’d believed that was his duty—as ruler of this nation, as an older brother, and as a human being.
But Jin Taekyung had kept his promise after all. He had given the finest physician beneath Heaven a hope brighter than ever before and sent him back.
*What more can I do for him to repay this debt?*
It didn’t matter. Whatever Jin Taekyung wanted, the Emperor would gladly give him.
With a quiet chuckle, the Emperor opened his eyes and slowly spoke.
“Tell Us. What must We do to live?”
For some reason, the Divine Physician’s smile turned awkward.
“What is it?”
“Well, you see... That is...”
“There’s no need to hesitate. We’ll trust your word and follow your instructions without the slightest doubt.”
“Forgive me, but even so, there may be a slight misunderstanding...”
The Emperor thought he knew what made the Divine Physician hesitate.

It happened all the time. He was the Emperor, ruler of all beneath Heaven. If anything went wrong with his health, the imperial physicians might have to answer for it with their lives. Even the finest physician beneath Heaven would worry about the consequences.
“Whatever concerns you, We assure you that nothing of the sort will happen. We swear by Our name... No, We swear upon the tombs of the late Emperors.”
The Divine Physician had been silently working his lips for some time. At the Emperor’s gentle reassurance, he finally spoke.
“Are those words truly sincere? Without the slightest falsehood?”
“Of course. From this moment on, We are a patient in need of your treatment before We are the Son of Heaven. We’ll trust you and follow your instructions, whatever they may be.”
“Very well. Since Your Majesty has said as much, I’ll speak frankly.”
In the next instant, the Emperor understood why the Divine Physician had hesitated—and how much he’d understated matters with *a slight misunderstanding*.
“The truth is, there’s no way to save Your Majesty.”
“To treat you, you must first die once. That’s where it begins—Your Majesty?”
The Emperor blinked. Somehow, his treasured sword was in his hand.
“Now, why would this suddenly—”
“Your Majesty? Your Majesty!”
“I’m sorry, Divine Physician. But We didn’t draw it of Our own will. The sword is moving by itself.”
“Your Majesty!”
The Emperor approached with his sword, offering an excuse even a passing traitor wouldn’t believe. The Divine Physician let out a shrill scream.
At the same time, he held out the thing he’d taken out earlier, just in case—the thing Jin Taekyung had given him a few shichen ago.
Or rather, he threw it at the Emperor.
*Clack.*
The Emperor reached out on instinct and caught it.
*Rattle!*
The cord binding it came loose, and bamboo slips unfurled, so old they had half rotted away.
“...What is this?”
His puzzlement lasted only a moment. As he made out the faint characters that remained, his eyes widened.
Maoshan Sect.
White Illusion Jiangshi Art.
It was the ancient root of a sect belonging to someone who no longer existed in this world, and who had treasured it dearly.
*Dududududu!*
The thunder of hooves rang out through the darkness.
The fine horses, said to carry the blood of sweat-blood horses, lived up to their reputation. Not one stopped for even a moment, and none of us—including me—slackened our reins.
“Deokcheong County is just beyond that hill!”
Ju Hwaran’s shout cut through the wind rushing past us.
We’d reached a second county just one shichen after leaving the Imperial Capital. It was good news, but I couldn’t smile.
*Not yet. At this speed, I can’t even be sure we’ll reach Anhui Province by noon.*
Neither our speed nor our time was nearly enough.
Even the imperial messenger eagles and couriers, who had left the capital about half a shichen ahead of us, might not arrive before the fighting began.
We had to hurry.
“Jeong Hogun!”
At my call, carried by internal energy, Jeong Hogun rode forward, his helmet pulled low.
“Speak.”
“How much longer until we reach Shanxi Province?”
Jeong Hogun thought for a moment as his horse raced onward.
“Ten days at the least. Fifteen at most.”
A difference of five whole days. And I knew fifteen wasn’t some leisurely estimate.
“Be more specific.”
“Fifteen days if we change horses on time at counties with relay stations ready and take only the bare minimum of rest.”
“Damn it. And ten days?”

Jeong Hogun trailed off. He glanced at the thousand Embroidered Uniform Guards racing ahead as one with their horses, then at the Fire Dragon Pavilion members following them.
“And we can forget about rest.”
His expression and tone were as impassive as ever, but I could hear the concern beneath them.
No, I couldn’t miss it, either.
*Reaching Shanxi Province won’t mean it’s over.*
We didn’t know exactly when Dark Heaven would invade. If Heaven was on our side, we’d arrive before the fighting began and have time to rest. But there was every chance we wouldn’t.
*If Dark Heaven has already taken Shanxi, or we arrive just as the battle begins...*
No need to finish that thought.
I spat out the curse that had been on the tip of my tongue for a while.
“Goddamn it.”
*Shhk!*
Jeong Hogun cut off a branch hanging over the road, spat out a leaf that had landed in his mouth, and replied,

His tone was so cold it made me dislike him on the spot. I felt my overheated thoughts cool down.
“Shit. This sucks.”
“Good. Are you done feeling sorry for yourself?”
“You cold bastard.”
“You can’t even show a little sympathy. No wonder you don’t have a single friend.”
“...That doesn’t sound like feeling sorry for yourself.”
“Of course it does. Just me feeling sorry for myself.”
At my firm reply, Jeong Hogun pressed his lips together.
The eyes visible through his helmet looked a little sad. That had to be my imagination.
*Anyway, if that’s how it is...*
Ignoring his reaction, I made my decision.
“We split up as soon as we pass through Deokcheong County. There are too many of us.”
“You mean divide the troops...?”
“All of you. And three people.”
“What?”
I pointed past him toward two figures racing ahead in the distance.
“Three of us are enough to get there first.”
Maybe you’ve heard of it.
Fire King on the left, Bow Saint on the right.

sentences.text: “I left a patient behind.”
At the Divine Physician’s answer, the Emperor’s eyes trembled.
*Could it be...?*
Suddenly, he found it hard to breathe.
Without realizing it, he clenched both fists.
A spark of hope kindled in a heart he’d thought he’d emptied completely.
He could feel his resolve wavering—the resolve to die on a battlefield, not in his bedchamber.
*No.
It can’t be.*
But deep down, the Emperor could only shake his head.
A crisis could drive a person to the edge of a cliff.
Hope was what finally sent them plunging into the abyss.
And so he forced himself to look away from the Divine Physician, who still watched him with a gentle smile.
“If you intend to join the army, I won’t stop you.
Before long, there will be countless casualties.
Your medical skills will be put to good use.”
“Your Majesty.”
Leaving the Divine Physician to finish whatever he’d meant to say, the Emperor quietly turned away.
Jin Taekyung, who had left to protect the Jin Family of Taiyuan, wasn’t the only one with no time to spare.
The Emperor’s life was truly drawing to a close.
In the brief time he had left—a few months at most—he meant to do everything he could.
For a better future.
For the precious people who would remain in this world after he was gone.
*That is my sole duty.*
The moment he steeled his resolve again, a quiet voice sounded behind him.
“I understand, Your Majesty.
I know how you feel.”
*Thud.*
The Emperor stopped as if his feet had been nailed to the ground.
The Divine Physician’s voice continued in his ear.
“A fleeting hope must frighten you.
Nothing is more painful than false hope.”
After a brief silence, the Emperor slowly turned.
The Divine Physician was still smiling at him.
“You understand well.”
“Through no choice of my own.”
“You must have met countless people standing between life and death in your work as a physician.”
“That’s not the only reason.”
“Then what is?”
The Divine Physician’s smile faded.
“A very long time ago, there was a young carpenter.”
“A carpenter?
Did he come to you because he had a fatal illness, too?”
“More precisely, he came to save his wife and children from an epidemic.”
“...His wife and children.”
“He carried his feverish wife and two children on his back in a wooden carrying frame.
For three days and nights, he climbed the mountain without sleep, looking for a skilled physician said to be staying in a nearby slash-and-burn farming village.”
The Emperor pictured the carpenter, drenched in sweat as he climbed the mountain, and muttered,
“That must have been hard.
Very hard.”
“As you say, it surely was.”
“But I doubt he even felt how exhausted he was.
He had hope he could save his family.”
The Divine Physician nodded.
“Yes.
He didn’t set down the frame and collapse until he reached his destination.
Then he lay sick for a day and a half.”
“So, did you treat his family?”
“Unfortunately, I couldn’t.”
The Emperor gave a small sigh.
The Divine Physician added bitterly,
“By the time I regained consciousness, it was too late.”
“That’s why I know how cruel hope can be.
What kind of despair waits at the bottom of that cliff.”
The Emperor fell silent.
He looked at the old physician before him, seeing the young carpenter who had lost his wife and children to an epidemic long ago and chosen a new path.
After a long while, he spoke.
“Then... then have you truly...?”
His voice shook with emotion he could not hide.
He forced out the question he’d wanted to ask from the start.
“Have you found a way to treat Us?”
Light returned to his eyes, and hope crept into his voice.
The Divine Physician bowed deeply.
“Yes.
With the help of Heaven—or rather, Young Master Jin—I was able to find the one and only path to survival.”
Jin Taekyung.
The unexpected name made the Emperor close his eyes.
In the darkness, he pictured Jin Taekyung’s face and offered him thanks he would never hear.
*You didn’t forget your promise to Us.*
He had not resented Jin Taekyung for leaving.
Even when he’d watched him walk away without a word about their promise, he’d felt only gratitude for all Jin Taekyung had done for the imperial house.
He’d believed that was his duty—as ruler of this nation, as an older brother, and as a human being.
But Jin Taekyung had kept his promise after all.
He had given the finest physician beneath Heaven a hope brighter than ever before and sent him back.
*What more can I do for him to repay this debt?*
It didn’t matter.
Whatever Jin Taekyung wanted, the Emperor would gladly give him.
With a quiet chuckle, the Emperor opened his eyes and slowly spoke.
“Tell Us.
What must We do to live?”
For some reason, the Divine Physician’s smile turned awkward.
“What is it?”
“Well, you see...
That is...”
“There’s no need to hesitate.
We’ll trust your word and follow your instructions without the slightest doubt.”
“Forgive me, but even so, there may be a slight misunderstanding...”
The Emperor thought he knew what made the Divine Physician hesitate.
It happened all the time.
He was the Emperor, ruler of all beneath Heaven.
If anything went wrong with his health, the imperial physicians might have to answer for it with their lives.
Even the finest physician beneath Heaven would worry about the consequences.
“Whatever concerns you, We assure you that nothing of the sort will happen.
We swear by Our name...
No, We swear upon the tombs of the late Emperors.”
The Divine Physician had been silently working his lips for some time.
At the Emperor’s gentle reassurance, he finally spoke.
“Are those words truly sincere?
Without the slightest falsehood?”
“Of course.
From this moment on, We are a patient in need of your treatment before We are the Son of Heaven.
We’ll trust you and follow your instructions, whatever they may be.”
“Very well.
Since Your Majesty has said as much, I’ll speak frankly.”
In the next instant, the Emperor understood why the Divine Physician had hesitated—and how much he’d understated matters with *a slight misunderstanding*.
“The truth is, there’s no way to save Your Majesty.”
“To treat you, you must first die once.
That’s where it begins—Your Majesty?”
The Emperor blinked.
Somehow, his treasured sword was in his hand.
“Now, why would this suddenly—”
“Your Majesty?
Your Majesty!”
“I’m sorry, Divine Physician.
But We didn’t draw it of Our own will.
The sword is moving by itself.”
“Your Majesty!”
The Emperor approached with his sword, offering an excuse even a passing traitor wouldn’t believe.
The Divine Physician let out a shrill scream.
At the same time, he held out the thing he’d taken out earlier, just in case—the thing Jin Taekyung had given him a few shichen ago.
Or rather, he threw it at the Emperor.
*Clack.*
The Emperor reached out on instinct and caught it.
*Rattle!*
The cord binding it came loose, and bamboo slips unfurled, so old they had half rotted away.
“...What is this?”
His puzzlement lasted only a moment.
As he made out the faint characters that remained, his eyes widened.
Maoshan Sect.
White Illusion Jiangshi Art.
It was the ancient root of a sect belonging to someone who no longer existed in this world, and who had treasured it dearly.

chapters.title: Chapter 943
paragraphs: “You can’t be serious!”
The moment my brief explanation ended, Hyuk Mujin cried out, his face stiff with shock. Then he sighed.
“But... damn it.”
He said no more, but everyone here could tell he’d accepted reality.
“If you rush ahead with your eyes fixed on what’s in front of you, you’ll trip over a rock. I know how hard this is for everyone, but for now, this is our best course.”
Namho addressed everyone with a serious expression.
He might have sounded like a seasoned elder, too—if he hadn’t been tucked into Taishan’s arms like a baby kangaroo.
“...I’ve been meaning to ask. Why are you riding like that?”
“Because it’s the most comfortable.”

Namho answered with unnecessary firmness, then added, “If I ride behind him, my ass feels like it’s going to get crushed. If I sit on his shoulder, a branch smacks me in the face every fifteen minutes. An old man like me would die before we reached Shanxi Province.”
Taishan, whose thighs were softer than a genuine leather sofa, nodded.
“Taishan save Namho.”
Since when had those two gotten so close?
I was still wondering why Taishan looked downright solemn when Namho smiled with satisfaction and pulled something from his pack.
“Good lad. Open wide. Here comes the five-spice pork.”
“Oh! Five! Spice! Pork!”
Right. I’d thought something was off.
I shook my head and eased my horse’s pace for a moment before speaking.
“Elder Namho, please make contact with the Murim Alliance as soon as you leave Zhejiang Province. They’ll be making preparations of their own.”
“I intended to do that anyway. As things stand, I’d only be a burden. I’ll try to lead the reinforcements and follow behind you.”
There wasn’t a single martial artist to be found in Zhejiang Province, where the Imperial Capital stood—let alone a sect.
But Anhui and Henan, which lay along our route to Shanxi Province, were another matter.
Henan was home to the Murim Alliance headquarters, of course. And closest to our current position stood a great power: the Namgung Family.
“Ilseom. Ma Pyo.”
At my call, Song Ilseom and Sama Pyo rode over and answered in turn.
“I’m listening, Pavilion Master.”
“I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve said this, but Sama is my surname, not my given name. Next time you call me...”
“I know. I’m doing it on purpose.”
At my firm reply, Sama Pyo muttered to himself, “Yeah, I thought so.”
“Enough. I trust you both know what you have to do.”
Song Ilseom and Sama Pyo were formidable martial artists despite their youth. Both nodded solemnly.
“Of course.”
“Trust us. Even if something goes wrong along the way, we’ll get everyone to Shanxi Province without a problem.”
I answered their determined assurances with, “Don’t fight each other.”
“Don’t start bickering in front of the Embroidered Uniform Guards. It’s embarrassing. Got it?”
“Answer me.”
The two of them stared at me with flat expressions, then let out quiet laughs. They both knew better than anyone that I was only joking.
“Understood.”
“I’ll try.”
“Did you hear that, Mujin?”
Hyuk Mujin, who’d been watching me in silence, nodded without a word.
He understood the situation and didn’t say anything more, but there was no hiding the emotions in his troubled expression.
He was hurt that I was leaving him behind without hesitation, and angry at himself for being nothing but a burden right now.
“Quit looking so miserable. Your face is ugly enough already—you’re making it worse.”
I let out a short laugh. Hyuk Mujin’s expression darkened further.
“Is that all?”
“Hm?”
“Why... haven’t you asked me to do anything?”
The smile I’d been forcing onto my face faltered.
His question caught me by surprise. I hadn’t expected him to think of it that way, and for a moment I didn’t know what to say.
After looking at him in silence for a moment, I answered calmly.
“Because you’ll do just fine without me asking.”
“Shanxi Province is where you’ve lived your whole life, and the Jin Family of Taiyuan is your second home. I know how you must feel right now.”
Hyuk Mujin’s eyes trembled as he looked at me.
*Crack.*
Both his fists were turning white.

He glared at the reins clenched so tightly in his hands they looked ready to tear and muttered, “Captain, you wouldn’t understand. What it feels like to have something you have to protect, but not the strength to step in. To be left helpless, doing nothing but watch.”
“...What?”
“No, forget it. I said something stupid. You’re the one who has it hardest right now... I sincerely apologize.”
I silently watched him bow his head, his face red.
I wanted to tell him I understood that feeling, too. That I’d felt it all too clearly, down to my soul shattering and my bones breaking.
But I couldn’t bring myself to say it.
Sometimes, comfort from the strong can make the weak feel even more powerless and wretched.
And the cruel truth that there are things you can’t protect even when you have strength was something Hyuk Mujin couldn’t understand yet.
So all I could do for the man who couldn’t lift his head, weighed down by shame and guilt, was say one thing.
“I trust you. More than anyone.”
“...Captain.”
“I’ll see you in Shanxi. No—at the Jin Family of Taiyuan.”
*Pat.*
I patted his trembling shoulder in farewell, then spurred my horse forward.
The wind felt colder than before. As I tightened my grip on the reins, hoofbeats approached and a quiet voice reached my ears.
“Hyuk Mujin didn’t mean what he said.”
It wasn’t just the hoofbeats drawing closer. I caught the scent of flowers and managed a smile.
“I know.”
“Do you know something?”
“What?”
I turned, puzzled, and saw Ju Hwaran beside me, her expression calm.
“Some smiles can look almost precarious.”
“I want more than anything to go with you, too, but I know I’d only be a burden, so I won’t complain. Still...”
Ju Hwaran smiled like moonlight spilling from the sky.
“When we meet again, let’s smile for real. Both of us.”
I watched her in silence, then spoke.
“We will. I promise.”
And in the next instant, I sprang from the saddle without a moment’s hesitation.
*Whoosh!*
Cold. The fierce wind whipped my hair around.
A weightless feeling swept through me as I leapt high into the air. Behind me, two pale figures cut through the dim moonlight in pursuit.
“Come on. Let’s hurry.”
At Jeok Cheongang’s low voice, the Bow Saint quietly nodded.
I—or rather, we—shot toward the rugged mountain range where no horse could travel.
*Whoooosh!*
“Well, that’s strange.”
At his companion’s sudden mutter, the bandit dozing against a tree opened his eyes to slits.
“What is?”
He’d just woken from a light sleep, so he was hardly going to sound friendly.
At the brusque voice of a senior bandit more than ten years his elder, his companion swallowed nervously.
“It’s nothing, sir. It’s just... the longer I sit here, the more something feels off.”
“Something’s off? I don’t see anything.”
The bandit tilted his head. His companion pointed at the sky.
“There aren’t any birds around today. It’s quiet as the grave. Doesn’t it feel a little unsettling?”
“Huh?”
The bandit’s eyes widened. Only then did he take a careful look around.
Now that he thought about it, it was true.
The sky was empty, and there wasn’t a single birdsong from the dense forest stretching in every direction, though the calls should have been constant.
*What’s going on?*
The question flashed through his mind, but his face soon settled into indifference.
What difference did a few missing birds make?

They might call themselves bandits, but they were only low-ranking lackeys. Their sole job was to watch their assigned stretch of mountain road until their eyes popped and contact the stronghold when travelers appeared.
“Maybe a hawk came around. Those birds don’t want to get snatched up and eaten in the blink of an eye, so they’re keeping their beaks shut.”
“Oh, come to think of it, I did see a few hawks fly by earlier.”
“Earlier? When?”
“About two hours ago, I think. Four or five of them, flying like arrows.”
The bandit must have missed them while he was asleep.
He stroked his shaggy beard and muttered, “That *is* a little strange. Hawks do whatever they please. I’ve hardly ever seen them travel in a flock.”
“Should I report it to the stronghold?”
“Report it? To the stronghold?”
“Yes. The deputy chief said to report anything unusual right away.”
“Not a bad idea. If you want to be chopped up alive.”
“The deputy chief’s probably fast asleep by now. Wake him, and you won’t like what happens. Disturb him over something like that and he might throw an axe at you.”
The bandit let out a long yawn and sprawled in the deep shade, stretching his arms and legs.
He still had a hangover from last night, and dozing against a tree had left his body stiff. This time, he meant to sleep until his back hurt.
He left everything to his younger companion, who still had plenty of enthusiasm.
“Quit trying so hard. Just watch for people. People.”
With the Double Ninth Festival not far off, merchants weren’t the only ones hoping for a big score.
The bigger the rice cake, the more crumbs there were to collect.
If they picked the right procession—a sizable merchant group or Escort Bureau—the tolls alone would fill the stronghold’s storehouse.
Just like now.
“They’re—they’re coming!”
“What? What?”
*Wham!*
At his companion’s hushed cry, barely a moment later, the bandit sprang up as if something had launched him and grabbed his axe in a panic.
Any trace of sleep was gone. His eyes shone like a hawk’s as he stared down the shadowed mountain road.
“Contact the stronghold. Hurry!”
“Y-Yes, sir!”
The bandit glanced after his companion as he ran off, then narrowed his eyes at the road.
He could see them. Clearly.
A few flags, swaying slowly.
And he could sense dozens of people.
*That idiot finally got one right.*
The bandit studied the flags passing between the branches.
Then he read the helpful lettering on the dark blue silk and learned the identity of these mouthwatering guests.
The Great Namgung Family.
