As I tightened my grip on the reins, hoofbeats approached and a quiet voice reached my ears.
“Hyuk Mujin didn’t mean what he said.”
It wasn’t just the hoofbeats drawing closer.
I caught the scent of flowers and managed a smile.
“I know.”
“Do you know something?”
“What?”
I turned, puzzled, and saw Ju Hwaran beside me, her expression calm.
“Some smiles can look almost precarious.”
“I want more than anything to go with you, too, but I know I’d only be a burden, so I won’t complain.
Still...”
Ju Hwaran smiled like moonlight spilling from the sky.
“When we meet again, let’s smile for real.
Both of us.”
I watched her in silence, then spoke.
“We will.
I promise.”
And in the next instant, I sprang from the saddle without a moment’s hesitation.
*Whoosh!*
Cold.
The fierce wind whipped my hair around.
A weightless feeling swept through me as I leapt high into the air.
Behind me, two pale figures cut through the dim moonlight in pursuit.
“Come on.
Let’s hurry.”
At Jeok Cheongang’s low voice, the Bow Saint quietly nodded.
I—or rather, we—shot toward the rugged mountain range where no horse could travel.
*Whoooosh!*
“Well, that’s strange.”
At his companion’s sudden mutter, the bandit dozing against a tree opened his eyes to slits.
“What is?”
He’d just woken from a light sleep, so he was hardly going to sound friendly.
At the brusque voice of a senior bandit more than ten years his elder, his companion swallowed nervously.
“It’s nothing, sir.
It’s just... the longer I sit here, the more something feels off.”
“Something’s off?
I don’t see anything.”
The bandit tilted his head.
His companion pointed at the sky.
“There aren’t any birds around today.
It’s quiet as the grave.
Doesn’t it feel a little unsettling?”
“Huh?”
The bandit’s eyes widened.
Only then did he take a careful look around.
Now that he thought about it, it was true.
The sky was empty, and there wasn’t a single birdsong from the dense forest stretching in every direction, though the calls should have been constant.
*What’s going on?*
The question flashed through his mind, but his face soon settled into indifference.
What difference did a few missing birds make?
They might call themselves bandits, but they were only low-ranking lackeys.
Their sole job was to watch their assigned stretch of mountain road until their eyes popped and contact the stronghold when travelers appeared.
“Maybe a hawk came around.
Those birds don’t want to get snatched up and eaten in the blink of an eye, so they’re keeping their beaks shut.”
“Oh, come to think of it, I did see a few hawks fly by earlier.”
“Earlier?
When?”
“About two hours ago, I think.
Four or five of them, flying like arrows.”
The bandit must have missed them while he was asleep.
He stroked his shaggy beard and muttered, “That *is* a little strange.
Hawks do whatever they please.
I’ve hardly ever seen them travel in a flock.”
“Should I report it to the stronghold?”
“Report it?
To the stronghold?”
“Yes.
The deputy chief said to report anything unusual right away.”
“Not a bad idea.
If you want to be chopped up alive.”
“The deputy chief’s probably fast asleep by now.
Wake him, and you won’t like what happens.
Disturb him over something like that and he might throw an axe at you.”
The bandit let out a long yawn and sprawled in the deep shade, stretching his arms and legs.
He still had a hangover from last night, and dozing against a tree had left his body stiff.
This time, he meant to sleep until his back hurt.
He left everything to his younger companion, who still had plenty of enthusiasm.
“Quit trying so hard.
Just watch for people.
People.”
With the Double Ninth Festival not far off, merchants weren’t the only ones hoping for a big score.
The bigger the rice cake, the more crumbs there were to collect.
If they picked the right procession—a sizable merchant group or Escort Bureau—the tolls alone would fill the stronghold’s storehouse.
Just like now.
“They’re—they’re coming!”
“What?
What?”
*Wham!*
At his companion’s hushed cry, barely a moment later, the bandit sprang up as if something had launched him and grabbed his axe in a panic.
Any trace of sleep was gone.
His eyes shone like a hawk’s as he stared down the shadowed mountain road.
“Contact the stronghold.
Hurry!”
“Y-Yes, sir!”
The bandit glanced after his companion as he ran off, then narrowed his eyes at the road.
He could see them.
Clearly.
A few flags, swaying slowly.
And he could sense dozens of people.
*That idiot finally got one right.*
The bandit studied the flags passing between the branches.
Then he read the helpful lettering on the dark blue silk and learned the identity of these mouthwatering guests.
The Great Namgung Family.

chapters.title: Chapter 944
paragraphs: The Great Namgung Family.
The moment the bandit made out the five characters embroidered on the fluttering flag, only one thought came to mind.
*Wait. What’s the Namgung Family doing here?*
Of course, it wasn’t impossible.
This mountain range lay at the southeastern edge of Anhui Province, and the Namgung Family was the undisputed ruler of Anhui.
Still, in more than ten years at the mountain stronghold, the bandit had never once seen the Namgung Family’s flag nearby.
*Why would they come all the way out to a backwater like this...?*
Even if a tiger stays in its cave, every beast knows who their king is, who owns this mountain.
The Namgung Family was that tiger.
Rather than hiding in a dark cave, it held Hefei, the heart of Anhui, and commanded dozens of sects.
One roar was enough to rally countless martial artists beneath its flag. That was the power and influence of one of the Five Great Families.
*There’s no reason for them to come into these rugged mountains.*
The range stretched from west to the distant eastern edge for hundreds of li. Why would the mighty Namgung Family leave the well-maintained main road and come here with only a few dozen people?
The bandit couldn’t make sense of it. But his fear, so fierce his heart felt ready to burst, was greater than his confusion.
*Goddamn it. What the hell are they hoping to scrounge up out here?*
Cursing inwardly, he steadied himself and carefully backed away.
Fortunately, he was several dozen jang away, on a hill thick with brush. Retreating without drawing attention wouldn’t be too difficult.
*Rustle, rustle.*
For a little over fifteen minutes, he edged backward, avoiding the leaves and branches on the ground.
Once he was sure he was clear of the danger of being spotted, he finally let out the breath he’d been holding.
“Hah... hah.”
His back was damp with cold sweat, and both legs trembled as if he’d suffered a stroke.
Only fifteen minutes or so had passed, but to a bandit who’d just escaped death, it felt longer than half a day.
“I-I’m alive. I’m alive.”
He gripped a nearby tree and sighed with relief. Then he suddenly felt sorry for himself.
*You pathetic fool. Just look at yourself.*
He didn’t regret becoming a bandit.
What could he do about it? He’d somehow been born, somehow lived, and somehow ended up here.
Still, if he was going to make his living this way, he should at least have joined a sizable mountain stronghold.
If he belonged to one of the Seventy-Two Strongholds under the Green Forest Alliance, merely seeing the Namgung Family’s flag wouldn’t make him fear for his life.
*If you’re going to be a servant, you might as well serve in a lord’s house.*
Had anything his drunkard father said ever hit so close to home?
The bandit wiped his eyes with his ragged sleeve and started back down the rugged mountain path.
Lord’s house or doghouse, either way, it was a house for a servant. He needed to get back to the stronghold and warn his brothers, who should be on their way here by now after receiving the signal.
If they ran into the Namgung Family when they weren’t even members of the Green Forest Alliance, they were as good as dead.
*Thank Heaven they’re still some distance away. If I head back now, we can all escape in time.*
Perhaps Heaven was moved by this noble display of camaraderie, because before another fifteen minutes had passed, the bandit encountered the fifty or so brothers led by their imposing chief.
More precisely, he found their chief sprawled out, while his brothers were, for some reason, lying with their heads pressed to the ground.
“I never meant to block your way, sir. So please, just...”
An unfamiliar back. An ominous feeling he couldn’t explain.
The deputy chief was earnestly explaining something to a bald man and a woman standing before everyone when he spotted the bandit watching blankly from some forty yards away. His eyes widened.
“Huh?”
Something was wrong. Very wrong.
The bandit sensed the danger and spun around. That was when—
*Poke.*
A finger prodded his cheek. An uninvited guest had appeared right in front of him and was studying him.
“Who are you?”
The bandit shuddered as if struck by lightning.
First, because he hadn’t sensed a trace of the man’s presence.
And second, because the stranger was much younger than he’d expected.
*A master...!*
A chill ran down his spine.
With his life hanging in the balance, the bandit barely managed to force out an answer.
“I-I’m Jang Il. My name is Jang Il.”
The world was definitely unfair.
The man was absurdly young, stronger than he’d imagined, and even looked like a courtesan’s pretty-boy brother. He asked again.
“Good. Jang Il. What do you do?”
“Trees. Trees.”
“I asked what you *do*. What the fuck do trees have to do with it? Are you a forest spirit? Jangquines, King of the Spirits?”
“N-No. I meant to say I’m a woodcutter, but...”
“Right, Jang Il. A woodcutter.”
The young man gave a small nod and glanced at the axe hanging from the bandit’s waist.
“You’ve got an axe, too. Because you’re a woodcutter, I suppose?”
“Y-Yes!”
“Then where’s your carrier frame?”
“...What?”
“Your carrier frame. You planning to haul all that firewood by hand after chopping it?”
“Well, I...”
The bandit hesitated, then hurriedly added, “Down below! I left it down below.”
“You left it down below. Sure, that happens.”
The young man muttered to himself and shrugged.
“Then let’s ask.”
The bandit didn’t have to ask who he meant. Before he could open his mouth, the young man called toward the thick brush.
“This woodcutter says he left his carrier frame down below. Did you happen to see it on your way up?”
At that moment—
*Whoosh.*
A gust swept through the bushes, and a half-gray-haired man appeared as if from nowhere. He shook his head.
“I saw nothing. Aside from one bandit fleeing in a panic, that is.”
“Oh, dear.”
The young man glanced at the bandit, who looked ready to faint, and clicked his tongue. Then he respectfully clasped his hands toward the middle-aged man.
“Thank you for letting me know, Great Hero Namgung.”
The Family Head of the Namgung Family, the Heavenly Thunder Sword, Namgung Ryong, clasped his hands in return.
“It’s good to see you again, Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung.”
No matter how vast the world, people whose paths had crossed were bound to meet again.
Of course, this meeting wasn’t entirely a matter of chance.
“We received word from the Anhui Provincial Office. We happened to be nearby, so we were able to get here quickly.”
I nodded at Namgung Ryong’s brief explanation.
“So the messenger eagle reached the provincial office.”
“About two hours ago. They were in quite a state over there, saying the Son of Heaven had issued the order himself.”
Well, Namgung Ryong wasn’t Namgung Gil-dong. He couldn’t just pop up in the east one moment and the west the next.

The imperial messenger eagle had entered Anhui two hours ahead of us and gone straight to the provincial office. After receiving the news, Namgung Ryong had immediately led his family members here. That was how it had happened.
“But how did you know where we were? Especially in a mountain range this damn huge.”
“No matter how vast it is, there are only so many paths. The terrain is rugged, but this is the quickest way through.”
An answer befitting the head of the Namgung Family, who knew Anhui Province like the palm of his hand.
Even so, a dark shadow hung over Namgung Ryong’s face as he looked at me.
“Is it all... true?”
There was no need to ask what he meant.
The air grew heavy. Then Jeok Cheongang spoke up.
“What, you don’t believe him?”
“Of course I do. I only wanted to make sure, because it’s a truth I can hardly bring myself to believe.”
Everyone felt the same way.
Bloodshed had already swept through Henan, Sichuan, and Yunnan, and even reached the Imperial Capital.
And before the stench of blood had faded, an even more terrible, far greater storm cloud was bearing down on us.
As the head of a family, Namgung Ryong had all the more reason to think of the many people who followed him.
“The Double Ninth Festival. The Double Ninth Festival...”
He muttered in a low voice, then looked at me with troubled eyes.
“My condolences. I never imagined they’d cross the northern grasslands and set their sights on Shanxi Province.”
After a brief silence, I spoke.
“They’ll be able to hold them off. They’re strong enough.”
Even as I said it, I knew the truth.
This was a lie meant to hide what I really thought—something closer to an attempt to comfort myself.
*The Jin Family of Taiyuan can’t manage it alone.*
Even Shaolin Temple, called the Mount Tai and Northern Dipper of the Murim, and the Sichuan Tang Clan, with its terrifying poisons, had suffered heavy losses.
Fortunately, Qingcheng, Emei, and the Nanman Beast Palace had kept their losses to a minimum and preserved their forces. But there was no denying that they’d faced a tremendous crisis.
And this time, it was Dark Heaven’s main force.
This wasn’t an attack to steal a divine artifact or destroy a single prestigious sect. It was a true invasion, meant to establish a foothold for an advance into the Central Plains.
*At least ten thousand. Maybe more.*
Even ten thousand—a staggering force—was only the minimum I was hoping for.
If everything so far had been a Mutated Gate, this was a Monster Wave.
Just as the Demonic Cult had swept through the Murim half a century ago with the Hundred Thousand Demonic Disciples.
*Damn it.*
My chest felt tight. I couldn’t stop thinking that if I’d found the missive left by the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord even a little sooner—or if I’d logged out before then—we might have gained some time.
*Of course, it was already too late.*
I’d lost three full days unconscious, and the Quest that appeared the moment I checked the missive in the iron chest had locked the door connecting me to reality.
It had taken away my last refuge, my place of rest, and forced me to move forward.
As if this were the only path I’d been given.
*Then... I’ll have to run. With everything I’ve got.*
I quietly clenched my fist and turned to Namgung Ryong, who seemed at a loss for words.
Holding on to a sliver of hope, I asked, “Where is the Azure Sky Sword King?”
Namgung Cheon, the Azure Sky Sword King.
A Supreme Peak master counted among the top three of the Ten Kings, and the Grand Family Head of the Namgung Family.

If he joined us and traveled to Shanxi, we could hold off even more enemies than I’d imagined. I already had two fighters at my side who could each take on ten thousand men: the Fire King and the Bow Saint.
But that brief hope vanished when Namgung Ryong answered with a quiet sigh.
“My father has been away from the family estate for a couple of months now.”
“Ah.”
“I’m afraid we don’t even know where he is. All we know is that he took on a mission at the request of Great Hero Mae Jonghak, the Alliance Leader.”
I hadn’t expected things to work out so easily. Still, I couldn’t help feeling disappointed.
“I see.”

“Still, as Family Head of the Namgung Family, I’ll help you and the Jin Family of Taiyuan. I’ve had fine horses, enough food, and a family member to guide you along the fastest route made ready, so you can set off at once...”
Just as Namgung Ryong was about to continue—
*Grrk. Krrk.*
With a muffled, strangled growl, a figure rose from the shadows.

chapters.title: Chapter 945
paragraphs: Grrk. Krrk.
What should I call that?
A groan? Or a roar?
Whatever it was, one thing was certain.
The burly man slowly rising to his feet was moving farther and farther away from the word *ordinary*.
“Who is that...?”
Namgung Ryong studied him with a questioning look.

He had no way of knowing. Before Namgung Ryong arrived, the man had happened upon Jeok Cheongang, attacked him without knowing what he was getting into, and been knocked unconscious with a single punch.
“He’s a bandit.”
“A bandit?”
“Yes. And he’s the head of the bunch.”
I tapped the top of my head. Namgung Ryong caught my meaning at once and nodded.
“I can see why that man was acting like their leader.”
His gaze grew more intent as he studied the man.
“Though I don’t know if an ordinary bandit chief could look like that.”
Ssshhh.
Hot breath spread through the air.
The man exhaled vapor through his clenched teeth. I stared at him—or, more precisely, at the translucent holographic window that had just appeared above his head.
**System** Lv. 60 Jang Sam
A painfully common name. A face that looked like a bandit at a glance.
But the change that had come over him in those few moments was unmistakable.
It wasn’t just the whites of his eyes or the hot breath pouring from his mouth. The number before his name proved it.
*His Level... went up.*
Of course, this wasn’t the first time I’d seen someone’s Level change.
Masters who had reached the realm of Returning to Simplicity, or something close to it, could control their qi freely. Even Qi Sense couldn’t accurately read their Level.
But this bandit chief was different.
He wasn’t a master of Returning to Simplicity, nor had he gained enlightenment and raised his Level that way.
*And people don’t jump twenty Levels all at once.*
A backwater bandit chief who’d been only Level 40 had suddenly leaped up twenty steps.
How was I supposed to make sense of that?
“This is way beyond anything I know. Care to explain?”
The moment I asked—
Whoosh.
A huge fist came down over my head with a heavy whistle.
Crash!
One step. I’d barely shifted to the side when the ground caved in, sending grass and dirt flying.
He could never have struck with that kind of force before he passed out.
I narrowed my eyes at him. Somehow, he’d acquired a considerable amount of internal energy, too.
*He’s completely lost it.*
I’d suspected as much from the whites of his eyes, but he’d all but lost his reason. Maybe he hadn’t even woken up of his own accord.
A man in his right mind wouldn’t attack me here unless he had a death wish.
“Raaaagh!”
“...Well, then.”
There was no helping it.
As he charged at me like a wild beast again, I slipped in close and gently extended my hand.
Tap.
My palm touched his chest.
At the same time, a faint heat—one I’d worked hard to suppress, over and over—burst out through my palm.
Boom!
With a sound like compressed air exploding, his eight-cheok frame shot away like a cannonball and slammed into a tree.
Kraaaash!
Beyond the thick cloud of dust, I grabbed his motionless body with one hand and dragged him back. The bandits’ eyes widened.
“We’re short on time, so I’ll keep this brief.”
As they stared in shock and fear, I went on in a low voice.
“Tell me everything you know. If you want to live.”
Every man lives with some dream tucked away in a corner of his heart.
It might be a red sports car with a price tag of a hundred million won, or a study that practically reeks of professional success.
I was no different.
As a teenager, I dreamed of owning a motorcycle. I wanted to put my girlfriend on the back and open it up.
Of course, I didn’t know then that ten years later, I’d still have no girlfriend.
Or that instead of straddling a sleek motorcycle or a red convertible, I’d be riding an eco-friendly, four-wheel-drive thoroughbred and saying this to a man:
“Hold my waist tight, you bastard. You want to fall off the saddle?”
“Y-Yes!”
“But don’t grab too hard. If you pinch me, you’ll die.”
“Eek! I’m sorry, I’m sorry!”
Thud-thud-thud!
The thunder of hooves mingled with a tearful voice.
Maybe Namgung Ryong and the authorities had already made arrangements, because nothing got in the way of us as we rode nonstop at full speed.
Only one thing bothered me: the guy behind me wouldn’t stop sniffling.
“So, Jangquines.”
Jang Il answered, sounding half resigned. He was the bandit who’d pretended to be a woodcutter who’d lost his carrying frame until I’d caught him at his real trade.
He’d been a bandit for more than ten years. He was at the bottom of the pecking order, but there was one thing that set him apart from the others.
“You’ve known that guy for ten years?”
“Yes. I’ve known him since I first got into this line of work. For a while, we were like blood brothers.”
“Brothers, my ass. You’re a bandit. What a load of bullshit.”
Jeok Cheongang had been listening as he rode beside us. At his candid opinion, the Bow Saint frowned and clicked her tongue softly.
“Stay out of it and let him finish.”
“What? Am I not allowed to talk to myself anymore?”
“You really haven’t changed. Apart from losing your hair, you’re just like you were back then...”
“Have you quite finished?”
Jeok Cheongang’s gaze turned icy. Lately, his hair had been slowly sprouting like shoots in spring, and he’d been tending to it with loving care. He made no attempt to hide his anger.
“That’s enough, you two. You, keep talking.”
Even as the two Supreme Peak masters exchanged cold looks, the horses kept running. Jang Il swallowed hard and continued.

“A-Anyway, I followed the chief from then until now. When he said we were moving the stronghold to Anhui Province, everyone called him crazy and left, but I followed him on nothing but faith and loyalty.”
“You moved the stronghold to Anhui Province?”
“Yes. We were near Hubei before, but one day the chief suddenly decided we were moving. Everyone was dead set against it.”
Jang Il smacked his lips, as if remembering the day, then went on.
“Truth be told, I didn’t say anything, but I was thinking of quitting this life and leaving before it was too late.”
“Why? Was moving the stronghold that big a deal?”
“Oh, you don’t understand. Packing up and going is only a bit of work. The problem is, Anhui has the Namgung Family.”
I frowned. Even at a glance, what Jang Il was saying didn’t quite make sense.
“That’s no reason. Wudang and the Zhuge Clan were in Hubei, where you were before.”
Jang Il immediately shook his head.
“It’s not about how many great sects there are. It’s about *which* ones are nearby.”
“Oh.”
“Wudang and the Zhuge Clan are relatively mild. Most of the time, they settle things without bloodshed. But the Namgung Family...”
Jang Il trailed off and shuddered.
“Maybe that’s why the martial artists of Anhui don’t show any mercy, either. If things go wrong, you’d better be ready to lose your head.”
It was so ridiculous I could hardly believe it.
Bandits, carefully weighing up which martial artists might come after them.

But there was something strange about the chief’s choice all the same. As if the Namgung Family weren’t enough, he’d set up his stronghold on the border between Anhui and Zhejiang, close to the Imperial Capital.
“When did you move the stronghold?”
“Probably... three months ago? Around then.”
“What about the other bandits? It sounds like everyone from your old stronghold ran off.”
“They say a pine caterpillar should stick to pine needles, but when we got here, we found some bold bastards playing bandit in Anhui without even belonging to the Green Forest Alliance.”
“So your chief brought them under his command?”
“That’s right. One day, he left me behind and went off alone. He came back having absorbed two small strongholds.”
Jang Il added sadly, “And here I am, still at the bottom of the pecking order.”
I had no interest in an aging bandit’s complaints. As the wind brushed through my hair, I thought, *Even if they were small, he took over two strongholds all by himself?*
Of course that was bullshit.
Before his Level went up, the man had been no more than a middling Second Rate fighter, relying on some tiny amount of internal energy—who knew how he’d built it up—and his natural strength.
*At best, he was on the threshold of First Rate. That wouldn’t be nearly enough.*

You had to be somewhere around Supreme First Rate before you could even talk about having a chance against dozens of people at once. And that was assuming your opponents were at least a notch below you.
“So he had something to fall back on after all.”
“Pardon?”
“The man you followed as chief. He wasn’t that strong, was he? What gave him the confidence to move to Anhui and bring two strongholds together?”
“Well...”
Jang Il hesitated, then nodded.
“I found it strange myself. He was strong by my standards, but his martial arts weren’t anything special...”
Anywhere under Heaven, a bandit who made a name for himself in his region eventually had two choices.
He could trust in his decent martial arts and swagger around until disciples of a great sect came to wipe him out, or he could join the Green Forest Alliance.
*For river bandits, it was the Yangtze River Channel League.*
No neighborhood shop could beat a corporation.

Become an officially recognized franchisee of the Green Forest Alliance, and you’d have to pay substantial taxes. But as long as you didn’t openly commit atrocities, you could avoid being hunted down by the great sects.
You went from being a mere bandit to part of a symbiotic system that at least followed a few basic rules.
*But that man fit neither category.*
After ten years without making a name for himself, he’d set up a stronghold within spitting distance of Zhejiang Province, where the Imperial Capital stood.
Even if he hoped to make a killing around the Double Ninth Festival, it made no sense.
Neither did the way he’d suddenly grown so much stronger.
*You couldn’t even call this a fortuitous encounter.*
Together, those strange events brought back a memory from more than a year ago.
*Pung Yang. Pung Yang, the Red Wind Band Leader.*
The leader of the mounted bandits who’d set his sights on the Mount Heng Sword Sect—no, on Shanxi Province.
And the one item that had given him such grand ambitions.
*The Temporary Strength Pill...!*

chapters.title: Chapter 946
paragraphs: Time is impartial.
To the living, the dead, and even things without form.

And so, the name that suddenly came to mind had begun to fade with time. If not for the fierce battle that day and the item I’d happened to get my hands on after winning, I might have forgotten it soon enough.
*The Temporary Strength Pill...!*
Was this what it felt like to be struck by lightning on the crown of your head?
The shock rattled my mind, and my body went rigid before I knew it.
*No way.*
My first reaction was denial. But I knew better than anyone why I wanted to reject the thought that had just crossed my mind: I didn’t want to believe it.
“What did that bastard—your leader—have?”
“Pardon?”
“Some secret that didn’t sit right. A strange item he didn’t have before. Whatever it was, remember.”
“G-Great Hero, what on earth do you mean...?”
Jang Il, who’d been clinging to my back like a leech, asked in a trembling voice.
Instead of answering, I fought to keep my grip from tightening around the reins.
We couldn’t stop here. We had to keep riding, if only for another moment. Stopping the horse now wouldn’t change anything.
“There must have been something strange. I’m sure of it.”
“P-Please, wait. Please calm down, Great Hero.”
Jang Il looked completely flustered. I was beginning to regret not bringing his unconscious leader instead when—
A dazed voice reached my ears. I whipped my head around to find Jang Il staring back at me, eyes wide.
“Come to think of it, at some point he started carrying a silk pouch everywhere.”
“A silk pouch?”

“Yes. I remember it clearly. A few months ago, an unlucky traveler passed through our stronghold in Hubei, and the chief took it from him instead of a toll. After that, he kept it close like it was some kind of sacred relic. I thought it might be precious musk or something.”
A traveler in Hubei.
A mysterious silk pouch the leader had kept close.
And his inexplicable behavior afterward.
“Um, was there something wrong with the pouch? I did wonder about it a little, since it didn’t have the distinctive smell of musk.”
I didn’t answer Jang Il’s question.
No—I couldn’t.

My ominous suspicion had just become a certainty. And I knew there was nothing more Jang Il could tell me. What had been inside the silk pouch, and who the traveler who’d owned it was—he wouldn’t know even decades from now.
*There’s no doubt. It was the Temporary Strength Pill.*

The Temporary Strength Pill did just what its name suggested: it drew out all the strength latent within the body. Having experienced its dangers firsthand when I fought Pung Yang, I could only grit my teeth.
*Crunch.*
“What is it?”
Jang Il wasn’t the only one who’d noticed something was wrong. I looked at Jeok Cheongang, whose face had gone rigid, and steadied my breathing.
“Do you remember what happened in Shanxi Province?”
“When do you mean?”
“I mean the mounted bandits who attacked the Mount Heng Sword Sect. I told you about them once before.”

Strictly speaking, Jeok Cheongang had arrived in Shanxi Province just after the Mount Heng Sword Sect affair had ended. But he was one of the few people who knew all about Pung Yang and the Temporary Strength Pill.
“...Then could it be?”
His eyes widened as he realized what I was getting at.
“Yes,” I said quietly. “It’s likely. No—given the circumstances, there’s no doubt.”
“Goddamn it.”
Jeok Cheongang let out the curse like a sigh. The Bow Saint, who’d been listening to us with a grave expression, spoke up.
“This is about that bizarre pill, isn’t it?”
“Don’t look so surprised. It may have been in the past, but it was only a year or two ago. I already knew about the Mount Heng Sword Sect and the Red Wind Band.”
Unfazed by my reaction, she continued.
“I know you were careful to keep it quiet, but unless you silence the witnesses, the truth has a way of getting out.”

The shock of remembering the Temporary Strength Pill had made me forget why the Bow Saint had chosen to stay by the Emperor’s side—and just how many eyes and ears the imperial court had scattered across this vast land.
“If you already know, there’s no need for a long explanation.”
A faint, inscrutable smile touched the Bow Saint’s lips as I regained my composure. It vanished as quickly as it had appeared.
“What happened at the Mount Heng Sword Sect raised questions for me, too. Especially after I learned more about Pung Yang, the leader of the Red Wind Band.”
Setting everything else aside, any martial artist would have had questions.

That day, in front of a fair number of onlookers, Pung Yang had displayed power approaching the Supreme Peak realm. He’d already become an accomplished Peak master, making him a formidable fighter in his own right. But manifesting Force, even imperfectly, defied common sense.
*Especially when the Head Elder, who’d reached the very limits of the Peak realm, could only show power like that after drawing on his innate qi.*
Learning martial arts was like climbing an endless flight of stairs. A beginner might skip several steps at once, but at the Peak realm, you had to give everything you had just to reach the next one.
Even Cheongpung, born with heaven-sent martial talent and strengthened at a dazzling pace, wouldn’t have skipped the steps laid out before him.
*But the Temporary Strength Pill makes that possible.*

Its effects were tremendous, its side effects terrible, and its power short-lived. Still, it could twist the natural order. There was no way the Bow Saint could have missed that after learning more about Pung Yang.
“At the time, a thought did cross my mind,” she murmured. “I wondered if Pung Yang—the man who died because of his greed—might be the one I’d been searching for.”
A question occurred to me.
If Pung Yang, not I, had survived that battle—and if he really had been the chosen one—what choice would she have made?
But I swallowed the question. What we were facing now was far too serious.
“It seems... someone is secretly distributing the pill Pung Yang used.”
Jeok Cheongang and the Bow Saint already knew who I meant by *someone*.
Dark Heaven.
The ones who had made the Temporary Strength Pill.
I didn’t know exactly when they’d begun preparing for this. But the fact that one had reached the hands of an ordinary bandit was no small matter.
“Are you sure?” Jeok Cheongang asked, his voice low. “From what this old man heard, its effects seem far too weak.”
The Bow Saint shook her head before I could answer.
“The bandit who stood in your way hadn’t even reached First Rate. Considering the change in him afterward, there are two possibilities.”
“What two?”
“Either its power varies according to the user’s level. Or...”
Her voice trailed off as she looked toward me.
“Or they reduced its effects,” I said, “and reduced the side effects along with them.”
A brief silence fell. Jeok Cheongang looked between us, his expression heavy, then muttered, “It must be the latter.”
“We can’t be sure of that yet.”
“No. Whatever explanation you come up with, it’s only wordplay to avoid facing reality.”
He shook his head and continued firmly.
“Everyone in this world wants power. Wealth, fame, strength—whatever form it takes, they want to stand above others. But everything has its price.”
Great power came at a great price.

And most people, however fiercely they wished for something, couldn’t bring themselves to put in the work to get it. They knew how hard that would be. To gain what they wanted in the future, they’d have to give up the comforts and pleasures they had now.
“But what if the price of a moment’s power were one they could bear?”
Then I understood why Jeok Cheongang was so certain—and what he was really trying to say.
“They didn’t make it just to bolster their own fighting strength.”
“How else could Pung Yang, who led a mere band of mounted bandits, or some petty mountain bandit get their hands on it? No—why would Dark Heaven reach out to the likes of them at all?”
No one would touch a bomb. It might go off at the slightest jolt, and its blast could tear you apart just for standing too close.
But what if it wasn’t a bomb? What if it was a campfire?

On a cold winter day, people wandering through the snow in search of something would reach toward it for warmth. Even if they got too close, they’d suffer only a small burn. They knew that much wouldn’t kill them.
A campfire anyone could reach toward. A trivial price for its warmth.
That was probably exactly what Dark Heaven wanted. This vast land was full of madmen eager to taste power, even at that small cost. And those called the orthodox faction would be no exception.
*Power anyone can obtain...!*
That was the true danger of the new Temporary Strength Pill.
Its alluring power would tempt people who’d spent ten years, even decades, stuck in the same place. In the blink of an eye, it would addict them and ruin them.
And at the same time, the Lord of Heaven could give greater vitality to his countless followers—or rather, to the people who were little more than disposable meat shields.
To the innumerable hordes of Dark Heaven surging like a wave toward Shanxi Province even now.

What had been inside the silk pouch, and who the traveler who’d owned it was—he wouldn’t know even decades from now.
*There’s no doubt.
It was the Temporary Strength Pill.*
The Temporary Strength Pill did just what its name suggested: it drew out all the strength latent within the body.
Having experienced its dangers firsthand when I fought Pung Yang, I could only grit my teeth.
*Crunch.*
“What is it?”
Jang Il wasn’t the only one who’d noticed something was wrong.
I looked at Jeok Cheongang, whose face had gone rigid, and steadied my breathing.
“Do you remember what happened in Shanxi Province?”
“When do you mean?”
“I mean the mounted bandits who attacked the Mount Heng Sword Sect.
I told you about them once before.”
Strictly speaking, Jeok Cheongang had arrived in Shanxi Province just after the Mount Heng Sword Sect affair had ended.
But he was one of the few people who knew all about Pung Yang and the Temporary Strength Pill.
“...Then could it be?”
His eyes widened as he realized what I was getting at.
“Yes,” I said quietly.
“It’s likely.
No—given the circumstances, there’s no doubt.”
“Goddamn it.”
Jeok Cheongang let out the curse like a sigh.
The Bow Saint, who’d been listening to us with a grave expression, spoke up.
“This is about that bizarre pill, isn’t it?”
“Don’t look so surprised.
It may have been in the past, but it was only a year or two ago.
I already knew about the Mount Heng Sword Sect and the Red Wind Band.”
Unfazed by my reaction, she continued.
“I know you were careful to keep it quiet, but unless you silence the witnesses, the truth has a way of getting out.”

The shock of remembering the Temporary Strength Pill had made me forget why the Bow Saint had chosen to stay by the Emperor’s side—and just how many eyes and ears the imperial court had scattered across this vast land.
“If you already know, there’s no need for a long explanation.”
A faint, inscrutable smile touched the Bow Saint’s lips as I regained my composure.
It vanished as quickly as it had appeared.
“What happened at the Mount Heng Sword Sect raised questions for me, too.
Especially after I learned more about Pung Yang, the leader of the Red Wind Band.”
Setting everything else aside, any martial artist would have had questions.
That day, in front of a fair number of onlookers, Pung Yang had displayed power approaching the Supreme Peak realm.
He’d already become an accomplished Peak master, making him a formidable fighter in his own right.
But manifesting Force, even imperfectly, defied common sense.
*Especially when the Head Elder, who’d reached the very limits of the Peak realm, could only show power like that after drawing on his innate qi.*
Learning martial arts was like climbing an endless flight of stairs.
A beginner might skip several steps at once, but at the Peak realm, you had to give everything you had just to reach the next one.
Even Cheongpung, born with heaven-sent martial talent and strengthened at a dazzling pace, wouldn’t have skipped the steps laid out before him.
*But the Temporary Strength Pill makes that possible.*
Its effects were tremendous, its side effects terrible, and its power short-lived.
Still, it could twist the natural order.
There was no way the Bow Saint could have missed that after learning more about Pung Yang.
“At the time, a thought did cross my mind,” she murmured.
“I wondered if Pung Yang—the man who died because of his greed—might be the one I’d been searching for.”
A question occurred to me.
If Pung Yang, not I, had survived that battle—and if he really had been the chosen one—what choice would she have made?
But I swallowed the question.
What we were facing now was far too serious.
“It seems... someone is secretly distributing the pill Pung Yang used.”
Jeok Cheongang and the Bow Saint already knew who I meant by *someone*.
Dark Heaven.
The ones who had made the Temporary Strength Pill.
I didn’t know exactly when they’d begun preparing for this.
But the fact that one had reached the hands of an ordinary bandit was no small matter.
“Are you sure?” Jeok Cheongang asked, his voice low.
“From what this old man heard, its effects seem far too weak.”
The Bow Saint shook her head before I could answer.
“The bandit who stood in your way hadn’t even reached First Rate.
Considering the change in him afterward, there are two possibilities.”
“What two?”
“Either its power varies according to the user’s level.
Her voice trailed off as she looked toward me.
“Or they reduced its effects,” I said, “and reduced the side effects along with them.”
A brief silence fell.
Jeok Cheongang looked between us, his expression heavy, then muttered, “It must be the latter.”
“We can’t be sure of that yet.”
“No.
Whatever explanation you come up with, it’s only wordplay to avoid facing reality.”
He shook his head and continued firmly.
“Everyone in this world wants power.
Wealth, fame, strength—whatever form it takes, they want to stand above others.
But everything has its price.”
Great power came at a great price.
And most people, however fiercely they wished for something, couldn’t bring themselves to put in the work to get it.
They knew how hard that would be.
To gain what they wanted in the future, they’d have to give up the comforts and pleasures they had now.
“But what if the price of a moment’s power were one they could bear?”
Then I understood why Jeok Cheongang was so certain—and what he was really trying to say.
“They didn’t make it just to bolster their own fighting strength.”
“How else could Pung Yang, who led a mere band of mounted bandits, or some petty mountain bandit get their hands on it?
No—why would Dark Heaven reach out to the likes of them at all?”
No one would touch a bomb.
It might go off at the slightest jolt, and its blast could tear you apart just for standing too close.
But what if it wasn’t a bomb?
What if it was a campfire?
On a cold winter day, people wandering through the snow in search of something would reach toward it for warmth.
Even if they got too close, they’d suffer only a small burn.
They knew that much wouldn’t kill them.
A campfire anyone could reach toward.
A trivial price for its warmth.
That was probably exactly what Dark Heaven wanted.
This vast land was full of madmen eager to taste power, even at that small cost.
And those called the orthodox faction would be no exception.
*Power anyone can obtain...!*
That was the true danger of the new Temporary Strength Pill.
Its alluring power would tempt people who’d spent ten years, even decades, stuck in the same place.
In the blink of an eye, it would addict them and ruin them.
And at the same time, the Lord of Heaven could give greater vitality to his countless followers—or rather, to the people who were little more than disposable meat shields.
To the innumerable hordes of Dark Heaven surging like a wave toward Shanxi Province even now.

chapters.title: Chapter 947
paragraphs: I’d known for a long time that danger was coming—danger we might not be able to contain.
I’d watched the enormous blaze called Dark Heaven draw closer with my own eyes.
But there was one thing I hadn’t known.
Another blaze was approaching from behind.
Its heat had begun spreading who knew when, burning through us from deep within, consuming our very organs.
*If the newly improved Temporary Strength Pill spreads throughout Murim...*
It won’t be a simple blaze anymore.
It’ll be a bomb.
A time bomb that’ll suddenly go off with a bang when the moment comes.
Just as drug addicts in the modern world keep using even when they know it’s destroying their minds and bodies, martial artists won’t be able to stop.
No. They’ll be worse.
Martial artists are lunatics who’ll do anything to get stronger.
Their desire to master martial arts is pure and primal—and that makes it more dangerous than anything else.
All the more so because that desire transcends the values of the orthodox, unorthodox, and demonic paths.
“They’ve... poisoned Murim.”
Jeok Cheongang’s grim murmur cut straight to the heart of our situation.
Poison.
He was right. This was poison.
The deadly poison of desire, which even the Myriad-Poison Ring couldn’t cure.
And among those present, only one person had yet to grasp that: a bumpkin mountain bandit.
“P-Poison? What do you mean by that, sir?”
Jang Il looked thoroughly confused.
But no one answered him.
“You there. Your ears working?”
At Jeok Cheongang’s abrupt question, the Namgung Family martial artists guiding us stiffened and replied.
“Of course, Great Hero Jeok.”
“The Family Head told us to treat you as we would him. Give us your orders whenever you like.”
“Orders, you say? Glad to hear it.”
Jeok Cheongang nodded, then gave me a look.
There was a reason I’d spoken about something so important out loud even with Jang Il here.
It was because of them.
*We need to get the word out as soon as possible.*
The unconscious bandit chief, who should be bound and on his way to the Namgung Family by now, was the key to this whole affair.
He’d already lost half his mind, so there was little chance he’d be sane when he woke. But an interrogation might still yield something important.
“Effective immediately, I’m changing part of your assignment.”
Namgung Cheon had sent four guides with us.
I looked at three of them in turn and gave them their new orders.
“One of you, go to the Namgung Family right now. Another, return to Great Hero Namgung and tell him what we’ve learned. And the last one...”
“To the Anhui provincial government?”
Quick to understand. That made this easier.
I nodded and continued.
“Tell the City Lord directly. He’s to mobilize every soldier he can, tighten security, and investigate everything connected to this.”
Dark Heaven’s improved Temporary Strength Pill had begun circulating months ago. No matter how discreet they’d been, a thorough investigation would turn up traces.
And if the City Lord himself, with at least ten thousand troops under his command, got involved, he could search even the remote places beyond the Namgung Family’s reach.
“I’ll relay your orders. But I’m not sure the City Lord will go that far for us...”
The Namgung Family martial artist let his words trail off. I thought I knew what he was getting at.
The government and Murim had stayed out of each other’s affairs since time immemorial.
The Emperor had declared war on Dark Heaven, but he’d done so by backing the Murim Alliance. This was a cooperative arrangement.
The City Lord, a servant of the Great Nation to his very bones, wouldn’t be pleased to hear this before he even understood what was really going on.
Especially when it came from martial artists. Officials and martial artists had spent years barely acknowledging each other, and this was an order in all but name.
“That’s true. He might not.”
The Namgung Family martial artist hesitated at my mutter, then shook his head.
“No. Don’t worry. Even if the City Lord objects, the Family Head can make a strong request in the Namgung Family’s name—”
“Well, there’s no need to go that far.”
“Pardon?”
“Do you have any paper? Oh, never mind. This’ll do.”
Riiip.
Leaving the Namgung Family martial artist blinking in confusion, I spread the strip of cloth I’d just torn off against the horse’s head.
At the same time, I gave a silent command.
*Open Inventory. Summon.*
Ding.
Along with a clear chime, a cool sensation reached the hand I’d been feeling around inside my robe with, just to keep up appearances.
“What’s that...?”
“Just a moment.”
The Namgung Family martial artist stared at the object in my hand. I ignored his questioning look and poured Scorching Yang Qi into it.
Hummm.
With a faint tremor, the ornately decorated silver plaque grew red-hot. So did the characters painstakingly engraved into it, no doubt by a renowned imperial artisan.
Ssssss.
The heated silver plaque met the dark blue silk.
After a few seconds of breathing in acrid smoke, I lifted it away. A blackened design and characters marked the torn strip of cloth.
*Great Marquis of Shangshan.*
“It’s a little messy, but they’ll be able to make it out, right?”
Silence fell.
The sound of hooves filled the space where no one answered. Before I knew it, everyone except Jeok Cheongang and the Bow Saint was staring at me, eyes wide.
“W-What on earth is this?”
“You didn’t know? It’d take too long to explain. Just take this to the City Lord for now, and make sure he knows it’s an order, not a request.”
The Namgung Family martial artists were still gaping at me.
“If he acts offended even after seeing it, tell him this. Word for word.”
“W-What should we tell him?”
I answered the trembling question without hesitation.
It was a rule that held true in Murim, the modern world, and even a fantasy world crawling with nest-building dragons.
“If I say do it, you do it.”
What rank did a City Lord hold in the official hierarchy?
The question briefly crossed my mind, but I knew one thing for certain. Now that I’d formally joined the ranks of the marquises, he was several rungs below me.
“Oh, one more thing. The reinforcements will arrive within a day or two at the latest.”
The mouths that had hung open moments ago clamped shut.
One of the silent Namgung Family martial artists forced out his voice.
“R-Reinforcements?”
“People from the Murim Alliance’s Fire Dragon Pavilion. And a thousand Embroidered Uniform Guards.”
“Stick close to the City Lord and keep an eye on him. If he seems really suspicious, tell them they can take his head.”

Anhui was close enough to the imperial capital that you could almost get there in a hop, skip, and a jump. The City Lord would have to be insane to harbor any other intentions. But that wasn’t proof Dark Heaven hadn’t gotten its claws into him.
“Is... is that really allowed?”
I answered the dazed question calmly.
“It is. I can.”
We were at war. Besides holding the exalted title of marquis, I was a Thousand Captain in the Embroidered Uniform Guard, which answered directly to the imperial household.
Unless he belonged to the imperial family—no, even if he did—I had more than enough authority to punish him.
And all of that authority and prestige came from the Emperor.
*The Son of Heaven put a sword in my hand himself. I’d better swing it without hesitation.*
I hadn’t accepted this sword to enjoy riches and glory or to look impressive.
I’d been given a sword and a title to cut down the enemies in my path and protect my people.
If reaching that goal meant dancing with a sword until I collapsed, I could do that.
“Now, let’s split up.”
At my abrupt words, the Namgung Family martial artists finally came to their senses. They’d been staring at me blankly even as their saddles jolted beneath them.
“We obey!”
Thud-thud-thud!
With a fervent shout that sounded like they’d forgotten who they worked for, three of them wheeled their horses around and galloped toward their respective destinations.
That left one guide to lead us to the border between Anhui and Henan—and someone we’d all forgotten about for a moment.
“I-I obey!”
The belated reply came from behind me.
I turned and met Jang Il’s eyes. The bandit wore a look of entirely unnecessary determination.
“For the sake of the realm, I’ll do everything in my power to help—”
“Get off. Unless you want to die.”
“Yes, sir.”
Anyone who’d lived through war even once knew.
The air around them. The wind. The sunlight. The people.
Everything was different from usual.
An inexplicably heavy, ominous darkness rippled through the world.
Perhaps that was why the old man couldn’t relax, even after waking from his first long, deep sleep in ages.
“Damn, the weather’s shitty today.”
Anyone who heard him mutter that would have scoffed and called the old man senile.
The sky beyond the lattice window was blue, and strong sunlight poured through the few scattered clouds.
But if that person were a martial artist—or simply lived in Hebei—they wouldn’t dare meet his eyes.
The old man scowling out the window was as renowned throughout the realm as he was enormous: a towering figure, and a living legend.
“Is nobody there?”
Even a beast’s quietest roar could make its surroundings tremble. The old man’s voice rattled the pavilion, and those nearby responded in an instant.
“Have you woken, sir?”
At the deep voice outside the door, the old man gulped down cold water and wiped his mouth.
“Where’s Cheolyeong, that bastard?”
“The Family Head is in the Inner Hall, attending a meeting.”
“A meeting?”
“Yes. It began two shichen ago.”
“Have they all gone mad? And nobody woke me?”
At the old man’s growl, the person outside the door caught their breath, then answered carefully.
“W-Well...”
“Got an excuse?”
“You said you’d rearrange our five viscera and six bowels if we woke you while you were sleeping soundly.”
“Oh.”
The old man scratched the back of his head.
Now that he thought about it, he had said that.
He hadn’t been sleeping well lately, and it had put him on edge. Then he’d finally fallen into a deep sleep and forgotten all about it.
“Damn it. I finally got a good long sleep, so I guess something must’ve happened.”
Clicking his tongue softly, the old man got up.
He knew what kind of men his eldest son, the current head of the family, and the senior members under him were.
If men with nothing but muscle between their ears had been sitting on their asses for two shichen, it had to be serious.
“Go to the Inner Hall. Tell them this old man is coming.”
The eyes of the towering old man—Peng Cheolhu, the Thunderbolt Saber King—grew deep and grave.

chapters.title: Chapter 948
paragraphs: Servants and maids hurried to clear away furniture broken and smashed in every direction.
Amid the wreckage, as though a typhoon had swept through the room, hulking men stood glaring at one another and breathing hard.

That was what Peng Cheolhu, the Thunderbolt Saber King, saw when he entered the Inner Hall’s grand conference room. He took in the scene, looked around, and said, “I’ll count to three. No more, no less. If you’re not back in your places by then...”
Whoosh!
Before he’d even finished speaking, dozens of hulking men scattered like the wind, returning to their original places.
All but one.
“You’re here, Father.”
The Thunderbolt Saber King frowned at the greeting from his eldest son, who was nearing seventy.
“You’re awfully late with your morning greeting.”
“I heard you were sleeping soundly...”

“Cut the nonsense. I thought you were finally ready to act like a proper person, so I handed over the Family Head position—and now you’re fighting with your own blood relatives? In this sacred conference room, no less, where we’re discussing matters of vital importance to the family!”
Peng Cheolyeong, the Iron Blood Saber and current Family Head of the Hebei Peng Family, silently took the booming rebuke before speaking.
“That reminds me of when you broke Third Uncle’s left arm. Here, in this sacred conference room where we discuss matters vital to the family.”
The Thunderbolt Saber King faltered, then replied sternly, “I was young and hot-blooded then.”
“That was last year.”
“...That can’t be right.”
“And that’s not all. The year before, Second Uncle dozed off for a moment during a meeting, so you punched him in the jaw—”
“Now, Family Head!”
Second Uncle rebuked Peng Cheolyeong for daring to talk back to his father, the Grand Family Head. Then he added, “It was my shin. I don’t know whose jaw you’re thinking of.”
“I’m sorry. I mixed them up. That was probably Fifth Uncle.”
Fifth Uncle, who had shrunk into a corner the moment the Thunderbolt Saber King appeared, muttered with mournful eyes, “Yes. Three years ago. When I woke up, two days had passed...”
“That’s enough. I get it. Let’s move on.”
Having failed to come out of the exchange with any dignity, the Thunderbolt Saber King shook his head and took the seat of honor.
Fortunately, the sturdy iron chair had survived intact. It had been made to withstand the Hebei Peng Family’s time-honored habit of throwing punches whenever the mood struck.
“Enough nonsense. Everyone, sit down. Tell me what you spent two shichen shouting and beating each other over.”
Peng Cheolyeong sat beside him and got straight to the point.
“Something’s wrong in the north.”
“The north? Why would the Murong Family suddenly be acting strange?”
The Thunderbolt Saber King’s assumption was only natural. To the Hebei Peng Family, *the north* had always meant the Murong Family.

At the far edge of this vast realm, the descendants of the Xianbei ruled Liaoning Province, a true frontier. Centuries ago, their ancestors had proclaimed themselves kings of a nation; now the family had long held its place among the Five Great Families.
“There’s no way the Murong Family is up to anything. You must have been given bad information.”
The Thunderbolt Saber King waved the matter away as though it wasn’t worth hearing. But Peng Cheolyeong’s next words made his expression harden.
“I wasn’t talking about the Murong Family.”
“What?”
If not the Murong Family, that left only one place.
The true north. A land of outlaws more lawless even than Murim, with schemes and blades lurking everywhere.
“Don’t tell me... you mean those barbarian bastards on the grasslands?”
“Yes.”
Peng Cheolyeong, considered the mildest of the Hebei Peng Family by blood, continued in a calm voice.
“The rumors coming from there are troubling.”
“They’re a vicious lot to the bone, but they’ve been quiet these past few years, haven’t they?”
The Thunderbolt Saber King was right. More precisely, peace and prosperity had begun to settle over the long-troubled grasslands about two years ago.
At the center of that change stood the Jin Family of Taiyuan, newly risen to power in the north.
“I heard there’s been no trouble since the Jin Family of Taiyuan formed that Seven-Route Army of theirs and swept through the place. Am I mistaken?”
“You’re exactly right. They went on a single campaign and pulled out the tooth that had been aching for ages.”
After taking control of the Shanxi Murim, the Jin Family of Taiyuan had moved with a speed and boldness that astonished even the Five Great Families and the Nine Sects and One Gang.
They absorbed sects that had once bared their teeth at them, along with Escort Bureaus and merchant houses. With that strength, they formed seven armed forces and swept across the grasslands.
The mounted bandits who regularly crossed the border to pillage and kill could not stand against the Seven-Route Army. Neither could the horse-riding tribes.
In fact, some of them had even rallied beneath the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s banner and reaped a handsome reward for their victories.
“Temur. Chinggen.”
At the foreign names that slipped from his son’s lips, the Thunderbolt Saber King narrowed his eyes.

He had devoted himself to martial arts since stepping back from the front lines, but he remained the Grand Family Head of the Hebei Peng Family in more than name. He remembered nearly everything discussed at the meetings he occasionally attended—even the names of barbarians whose faces he had never seen.
“Those two who sided with the Jin Family of Taiyuan and became Great Chieftains. Am I right?”
“Yes. I hear they’re called khans on the grasslands.”
“Khan or can, I don’t care. What matters is what those bastards are doing.”
The Thunderbolt Saber King tapped the table with fingers like iron rods, lost in thought.
Temur and Chinggen had risen to power on the grasslands thanks to their alliance with the Jin Family of Taiyuan. If they were behaving suspiciously, there were two possible reasons.
They had grown dissatisfied with what they possessed and wanted more.
Or...
“What are the chances they’ve joined hands with Dark Heaven? I could tear those bastards to pieces and still not be satisfied.”
“We don’t know for certain yet,” Peng Cheolyeong said quietly. “But the evidence suggests they’ve conspired with Dark Heaven.”
The Thunderbolt Saber King let out a low groan to himself.
*Those bastards wouldn’t suddenly try this unless they’d lost their minds. Not when they know Fire King—that crazy old man—is standing right behind the Jin Family of Taiyuan.*

Everyone knew of Jeok Cheongang’s ties to the Jin Family of Taiyuan. Rumor held that fear of the Fire King was why Temur and Chinggen had allied with the family, even betraying some of their own people to build the power they now held.
*And now they’re going to stab him in the back like this? It makes no sense.*
Jeok Cheongang was hellfire itself: a blaze that died down only after reducing everything to ash.
The Thunderbolt Saber King was prouder than anyone, but he hated even the thought of becoming the Fire King’s enemy in earnest.
*Someone’s backing them. There has to be.*
He studied his eldest son.
“You have a reason for thinking this. What’s your evidence?”
“About two years ago, we placed people we could trust on the grasslands.”
“Informants... You used your head.”
“The situation there was still unstable. We made our move when the new trade routes opened.”
Opening a route meant letting people in.
After the Seven-Route Army’s campaign, led by the Jin Family of Taiyuan, more than fine ceramics and jewelry passed along the grassland trade routes.
People.
New kinds of people the lawless grasslands had not seen for a long time.
Some of those who filled the vacuum there included informants from the Hebei Peng Family.
“Recently, a few of them sent word that the barbarians on the grasslands are gathering.”
“How many?”
“At least ten thousand.”
“...What? Ten thousand?”
“Father.”
Peng Cheolyeong struggled to speak at the sight of the Thunderbolt Saber King staring at him, eyes wide.
“That’s only the number of troops confirmed so far.”
For a moment, the Thunderbolt Saber King doubted his ears.
Ten thousand. A full ten thousand.
Not a rabble, either, but warriors of a horse-riding people who had once thundered across the continent. Men born on the open plain who died in the saddle.
*And that may not even be all of them...*
He looked down at his fist. He had clenched it so tightly that his knuckles had gone white.
He could almost see the countless riders charging as one, reins in one hand, bows and lances in the other.
Then fury surged from deep in his chest and blotted out the vision.
“Enough!”
Whoom! Crash!

A powerful wave of qi swept through the room with a thunderous boom. The Thunderbolt Saber King smashed the huge iron table with one punch and rose, glaring at Peng Cheolyeong—no, at everyone in the conference room.
“Were you going to decide a matter this grave without me? Have you all lost your minds?”
Crrrreak.
The giant’s power pressed down from every side. The old Grand Family Head’s anger shook the conference room as though a typhoon had struck it.
Then Peng Cheolyeong spoke.
“I had to hear everyone’s opinions before I told you.”
“You fool! The family’s survival is at stake!”
His eldest son remained calm—the son he had trusted enough to make Family Head—but the Thunderbolt Saber King’s anger would not subside.
Ten thousand already confirmed. If the barbarian force grew to tens of thousands and entered Hebei in fifteen days—or even in a few days—there would be no containing it.
“How dare you...”
Betrayal and disappointment burned through him.
Then Peng Cheolyeong’s subdued voice reached his ears.
“Please forgive me. I couldn’t risk Hebei Peng Family blood being spilled over a hasty decision. That’s all.”
“What does that—”
His trembling body went still.
Only then did the Thunderbolt Saber King sense something was wrong. He slowly scanned the faces around him and realized what had struck him as familiar about Peng Cheolyeong’s words.
*They aren’t after our family!*
The realization flashed through him like lightning.

Of course. If the grassland forces were already marching south toward Hebei, no one would still be sitting in this conference room. They would be mobilizing the family’s forces and the entire Hebei Murim, preparing for battle as fast as they could.
*Then... surely not?*
His face went rigid.
“Shanxi. It’s Shanxi Province.”
He had spoken almost to himself, but Peng Cheolyeong quietly nodded.
“When will those goddamn bastards set foot in Shanxi Province?”
Someone answered in a grave voice.
“We expect them within seven days at the latest.”
“Do they—the Jin Family of Taiyuan—know?”
“Yes,” Peng Cheolyeong said quietly. “They’re already preparing for battle.”
The Thunderbolt Saber King groaned and raised his head. Beyond the window, dark clouds now filled what had been a blue sky.
Fewer than ten days remained until the Double Ninth Festival.
